A 2B decision model on the app server answers the short, easy questions, and anything it’s unsure about, or anything too long for it, goes to DeepInfra. Strands Decider 2B reads 4,096 tokens by default, so long states are an automatic escalation:

def route_ticket(ticket):
    a = ask(ticket, QUEUE, url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/systemone")["queue"]
    if max(a["probabilities"].values()) >= 0.85 and len(ticket) < 8000:
        return a["choice"], "local"
    q = QUEUE["queue"]
    choice, conf = decide(ticket, q["instructions"], q["criteria"],
                          model="deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash", priority=True)
    return choice, "deepinfra"copy

This is the private lane from the review’s model router, pointed the other way. There, the local model kept sensitive prompts off the cloud. Here, it keeps the fast, confident decisions off the network and spends DeepInfra calls on the cases a 2B model is more likely to get wrong. The 0.85 threshold held up on the bake-off set. Strands put 71 of its 144 answers at or above it, and all 71 were right. Sending the other 73 to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash scored 139 of 144 overall, Jev’s number, with half the decisions never leaving the machine. That’s one run on three-option questions, so recheck the cutoff on your own labels. The same two-model shape for agents is in why two-tier agents need two models.

Which Jev alternative to pick

  • Go with Jev if you need a hosted p95 under 400 ms, your inputs are English text, and a closed API is acceptable. It also had the best-calibrated confidence in the bake-off, at a price within a fraction of a cent of the cheapest lane.
  • Go with DeepInfra structured outputs if you already call an open model there. It’s the same key, the same SDK, and one more schema, at $0.013 to $0.017 per 1,000 decisions, and small open-weight models keep that price low as volume grows. Switch to echo scoring when the job needs a probability on every option.
  • Go with Strands Decider 2B or OpenJev for gates on the request path, or for data that can’t leave the machine.
  • Go with Laya if you need 100-plus languages from its multilingual checkpoint, or CPU-only hosting.
  • Go with Kev if you prototyped against Jev and want the same wire format on your own GPU or Mac.
  • Go with AnyJev or SemIf if you already self-host an open model on vLLM or llama.cpp and want per-option probabilities without training anything.
  • Go with Clef on Workers AI or the OpenAI Decisions API if your decisions depend on images. Only Clef reads video.

FAQ

Is there a free Jev alternative?

Yes. All six open projects above are free under Apache 2.0 or MIT, and Strands Decider 2B, Laya, and OpenJev’s 1.7B model run on a laptop. You pay for hardware instead of tokens, though Jev is close to free at small volume anyway.

Can I use a regular LLM instead of Jev?

Yes, if you constrain its output. An enum schema makes any supported open model pick from a fixed list, and logprobs give a confidence for the pick. Expect more latency than a dedicated decision model (568 ms for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash against Jev’s 245 ms in our test), and turn thinking off on hybrid reasoning models.

Does OpenAI’s Decisions API return probabilities?

Yes. OpenAI’s Decisions guide says a choice answer carries a probability for each option plus a separate confidence field. We haven’t measured how well calibrated those probabilities are, so check them against your own labeled examples before a threshold in your code depends on them.

Can a Jev alternative run on CPU only?

Yes, slowly. Strands Decider 2B runs on CPU at about 1.6 seconds per short input on an eight-thread Xeon in published tests, and 16 to 18 seconds at around 3,000 tokens. That suits batch jobs, not gates a user waits on.

Start with the decider you already have

Even the fastest decision model needs something to write the reply. If that something is an open model on DeepInfra, start there: Qwen3.5-9B on DeepInfra, an enum schema, and the DeepInfra docs. To try the model you already run, change the model string; the schema stays the same, and so does the guarantee that every answer comes from your list. Tell us what you route with it at feedback@deepinfra.com, on Discord, or on X.

Related articles

It climbed to the top of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, outperforming several closed models that cost significantly more to run. For an open-weight model, especially one as large as 2.8 trillion parameters, that was […]</p>

The architecture utilizes […]</p>

item.title: [Mistral AI] Le Chonk: Built for Coders, Trusted by Defenders.
item.content:encoded:
Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk)

Built for Coders,Trusted by Defenders.

Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk)Built for Coders,Trusted by Defenders.

Copy url to clipboardCopied

Thinking

Summary

Mistral released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model, now available with improved coding, cybersecurity, and reasoning efficiency. It leads open-weight benchmarks in coding and defensive security while offering three reasoning modes for cost-performance balance. Fully open-weight and European-trained, it empowers sovereign AI with customizable, self-hosted deployment options.

We release the weights of Le Chonk, advancing the frontier of open models in agentic coding and cybersecurity.

Earlier this month, we released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), our flagship 1-trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model, in public preview. The response to the preview has exceeded our expectations, and we're grateful to our developer community, early-access customers, and partners for their support, collaboration, and feedback.

Since then, we've put that feedback to work while continuing to scale reinforcement learning, driving massive improvements in coding and defensive cybersecurity. Gains continue to accelerate, with no signs of saturation.

Today, we're releasing the weights of this improved Mistral Large 4. The new model also features substantial gains in reasoning efficiency that give developers greater performance while lowering inference costs.

Mistral Large 4 ranks as the best open-weight model for coding and among the world's most capable open models overall. Trained from scratch on European infrastructure with clear lineage from inception to release, it gives organizations a trusted foundation for Sovereign AI

Mistral is defining the sovereign AI category and leading the open frontier. We're committed to building the world's most capable models and releasing them openly, giving developers, enterprises, and institutions the power to own, customize, and control their AI.

Built for the Builders.

Mistral Large 4 entered public preview with strong results across leading coding benchmarks. Just three weeks of additional reinforcement learning have since propelled it to the forefront of open-weight coding, taking the lead on FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench while matching the best open-weight models on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with substantially greater token efficiency.

On Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark, which assesses end-to-end code quality and whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change, Mistral Large 4 leads with a score of 19.7%.

Cognition - FrontierCode 2.0

Pushing the pareto frontier for agentic coding.

Mistral Large 4 delivers frontier coding performance with significantly fewer tokens, making sophisticated coding agents more economical to run at scale.

On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral Large 4 scores 48%, effectively tied with the leading open-weight model, GLM-5.3, while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average.

Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index vs. Token Efficiency

  • Mistral
  • Other models

Coding Agent Index scores and token efficiencies for reasoning levels available on Artificial Analysis

The gains extend to terminal-based coding workflows. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Mistral Large 4 improved by 13 percentage points to 41% compared to its public preview, taking the lead among open-weight models while reducing output tokens by 30%.

Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index - Terminal-Bench 4.0

To give developers greater control over this tradeoff between performance and cost, Mistral Large 4 now supports three reasoning modes:

ModeRecommended Use
LowSimple tasks; replaces ‘None’ reasoning mode
MediumEveryday tasks
High (default)Hardest use cases requiring high precision and thorough reasoning

Beyond benchmarks, Mistral Large 4's coding capabilities are validated by human preference. In Surge Code's blind pairwise evaluations, Mistral Large 4 was preferred over leading open-weight models including GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, ranking behind only Claude Opus 5.5 among the models evaluated.

Surge Code - Human preference on code

Blind side-by-side win rates against other models

  • Mistral Large 4 win
  • Other model

Share of prompts where graders preferred Mistral Large 4's answer over the opponent's.

Built for the Defenders.

Since its preview, we've been working with leading cybersecurity vendors to evaluate Mistral Large 4 in real-world environments to test Mistral Large 4’s strengths in vulnerability reproduction and patching.

Mistral Large 4 scores 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which measures a model’s ability to discover vulnerabilities in a codebase, reproduce and validate them, and patch them without breaking existing functionality. Crucially, Mistral Large 4 handles these legitimate defensive security tasks without unnecessary refusals.

Artificial Analysis - Cyber Index

Safety has improved alongside capability. Our model’s built-in guardrails distinguishes between defensive and malicious, offensive cybersecurity tasks. It retains strong performance on Cyber benchmarks, while achieving an average refusal rate of 96.6% on malicious cyber requests, the highest we measure among open models.

Refusal of harmful cyber requests

Average refusal on the cyber-related prompts of JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm

Here’s what global leaders in cybersecurity have to say about Mistral Large 4:

Testing by Booz Allen demonstrated the success of the European Mistral Large 4 model against our internal benchmark for source code security analysis. The model was able to match vulnerability detection recall rates against other frontier cyber models with a compelling cost curve. And, Mistral's support for model customization and data-sovereign deployment also lets us tailor it for our mission needs and client environments with strict data-residency requirements. We look forward to working with Mistral to strengthen critical infrastructure around the globe.

Brad Medairy, President National Cyber at Booz Allen Hamilton

Organizations that treat transparency and openness as strengths are positioned well as AI becomes central to security operations. Open-weight cybersecurity models extend that transparency to enterprises and governments that need to host and customize AI under their own control, and they allow researchers to study how these models behave, including where they could be misused. As adversaries increasingly use AI to accelerate their operations, we aim to work alongside model developers such as Mistral to help security teams build on that control, establishing a foundation for resilience by design rather than reactive threat management.

Amy Chang, Head of Cisco's AI Threat Intelligence and Security Research

When threats move at machine speed, human defense cannot keep pace. Worse, a defense you don’t control isn’t defense—it’s exposure. Security teams perform best when they take the steering wheel. Mistral's ML4 lets defenders audit the architecture, deploy on their own infrastructure, and keep full sovereignty. Resilience starts with autonomy, and open-weight models help give organizations the control to lead their own defense."

Stephanie Cohen, Chief Strategy Officer at Cloudflare

Powerful AI models alone won't tip the scales in cybersecurity. It takes deep security expertise, real-world threat intelligence, and rigorous testing. Our work with Mistral Large 4 tests how well frontier AI can reason through complex vulnerabilities, accelerate remediation, and ensure defenders move faster than adversaries.

Dr. Bartley Richardson, Chief AI and Autonomous Systems Officer, CrowdStrike

Elastic gives security teams the freedom to bring the AI they trust to the data they control, including Mistral’s open models, which are supported on Elastic Security today. We’ve already evaluated ML4 against real cybersecurity workloads, where models need to reason across complex data to help analysts make informed investigation and response decisions. This demonstrates the partnerships we are building to deliver powerful, open-weight models combined with the security context, transparency and control our customers demand.

James Spiteri, Senior Director, Product Management, Elastic

ENISA is experimenting with closed and open weight models in order to better understand their cyber capabilities. Open-weight models allow organisations to keep control of the technology their resilience depends on. ENISA access to and are testing Mistral Large 4 to identify security vulnerabilities, to audit code and analyse defensive logs.

Laura Heuvinck, Head of Communications of ENISA

We believe open-weight AI models have an important role to play in advancing cybersecurity by giving organizations greater flexibility, choice, and control. Innovations like Mistral Large 4 represent promising steps forward in AI's potential to transform cyber defense. We see continued AI innovation as an important opportunity to strengthen cybersecurity and help organizations navigate an evolving threat landscape.

John Whittle, Chief Operating Officer at Fortinet

Open models let security researchers and developers inspect, adapt and build on AI. Mistral is expanding what the ecosystem can build, and our collaboration on NVIDIA accelerated infrastructure helps developers put these models to work.

Kari Briski, VP of Open Models and Software, NVIDIA

As threats become ever faster, industrialized and now automated, defense must operate at a different scale. Volume, speed, trust: these are the three challenges facing cybersecurity in the age of AI. With Mistral AI, we are building European cyber AI, trained by our experts and operated under their control. By combining the power of AI, the expertise of our teams and our Cyber Threat Intelligence, we are accelerating our response so that we can protect more broadly, more quickly and with trusted European technology.

Hugues Foulon, CEO of Orange Cyberdefense

Rubrik supports Mistral and the push for ‘sovereign AI,’ to give European governments and regulated industries a credible option that does not route their data to other countries. Customers want model choices, including open-weight and private models, to support data residency, latency, cost and capability requirements. As part of our focus to deliver cyber resilience and speed recovery from both AI-powered attacks outside an organization and internal agents, we’ll continue rigorous cybersecurity testing with Mistral Large 4 and work closely together to serve evolving regional demands.

Anneka Gupta, Chief Product Officer of Rubrik.

As enterprises bring AI into production, they increasingly want models they can run on their own terms, with clear visibility into model behavior, data access, and agent permissions. Mistral Large 4 brings strong cybersecurity and technical reasoning to open weight AI, and many European enterprises are already embracing it as their sovereign model of choice. Zscaler Security for AI offerings, delivered on our sovereign Zero Trust Exchange in Europe, now integrate with Mistral, helping organizations continuously test their AI deployments, map what every model and agent can reach, and enforce policy inline. Together, we are empowering enterprises to adopt sovereign AI with the visibility, control, and data protection they need to innovate securely.

Dhawal Sharma, EVP of AI and Data Security, Zscaler

In the time since the preview, we carefully monitored cybersecurity-related use in our live traffic. Though we observed the model refusing to comply with black-box attacks against live targets, we see a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks. We are modifying our guardrails accordingly, and will continue updating them in the months to come.

We are also providing enterprise design partners such as Orange Cyberdefense, with preview access to a specialized variant of Mistral Large 4 optimized for advanced cybersecurity workflows, including penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, and red-teaming. Access is subject to rigorous vetting and contractual safeguards, with testing restricted to owned or explicitly authorized systems in controlled environments.

Meanwhile, customers are tailoring Mistral Large 4 with proprietary security data, policies, detection logic, and threat environments using Mistral Forge. For well-defined cybersecurity tasks, it can be further optimized into smaller, task-specific variants for greater accuracy, making security applications more effective.

Learn more about sovereign AI for cybersecurity and how to work with us.

Built for Work.

Mistral Large 4 has continued improving on a range of broad enterprise-use metrics.

For finance-related work, we improved the model’s ability to perform real-world workflows, especially ones involving the creation and editing of spreadsheets for finance and accounting use cases. This is reflected in our Finch scores climbing to 73.3%, second only to Kimi K3 for open models.

FinWorkBench (Finch)

Web browsing is a critical part of a majority of knowledge work. Our RL pipeline enabled us to reach 84.5% on BrowseComp (starting from an SFT checkpoint that was achieving 75%). This brings Mistral Large 4 at a higher performance than models like GLM-5.3 or DeepSeek Flash 4.1 1017.

Web browsing - BrowseComp

Agents deployed by an organization need to be secure. Whether deployed to internal members or external users, agents shouldn’t open you up to threats like system prompt exfiltration or malicious code injection. RL increased our gains on the B3 Agent Security Benchmark, with Mistral Large 4 resisting 97.1% of attacks vs 93.3% in Preview. This places it at the top of the OSS frontier, meaning anyone hosting the model can run a safe agent without additional tuning.

B3 Agent security benchmark - Attack resistance

This major investment by Mistral AI reinforces the choice La Banque Postale made over a year ago and underscores the relevance of the long-term strategic partnership we are building together: supporting the emergence of an open and sovereign European AI leader. For a public and citizen bank, technological sovereignty is not optional; it is a key prerequisite for maintaining our customers' trust. The introduction of this open model unlocks new opportunities and use cases. By partnering with Mistral AI, our ambition is to combine the best of human expertise and digital technology to deliver an enhanced experience of both customers and employees over the long term.

Zakaria Moursli, Executive Vice President, Operational Performance, Payments and Digital Services, La Banque Postale

See it in Action

Cyber Vulnerability Triage: an agent reads incoming vulnerability reports, investigates the source code and product context, reproduces the flaws in an isolated sandbox, then writes and iterates on a patch until a canary exploit no longer works.

Agentic webdev: with no human help, Mistral Large 4 builds Orbital Trace, a live 3D map of roughly 19,000 satellites and debris pieces orbiting Earth. It pulls real tracking data, writes the app, uses it in a browser to catch its own bugs and slowdowns, then fixes what an independent reviewer flags until all requirements pass.

Quantum chemistry solver: Mistral Large 4 writes, from scratch, software that calculates where electrons sit in a molecule, and checks its answers against a standard chemistry tool. It then builds a 3D page around it: pick a molecule such as benzene or water, drag a slider to pull it apart, and watch the electrons regroup as the bond breaks.

Built for Sovereignty.

As organizations build AI around their knowledge and workflows, sovereignty means that they retain control of the models they depend on and the intelligence they create.

With Mistral Large 4, that control begins with the model itself. Organizations have the ability to inspect, customize, and deploy the model on their own infrastructure. They can use and improve Mistral Large 4 without depending on Mistral to serve it through an API. Mistral Large 4 was developed and trained from scratch in Europe, giving organizations clarity about the origins of the technology they’re building on.

Control also extends to how AI operates inside an organization. Organizations can customize Mistral Large 4 around their proprietary data with Mistral Forge, and they can build, govern, and improve the resulting agents and applications using Mistral Studio. Mistral’s Applied AI experts can work alongside customer teams to build and deploy these tailored systems. Through that work, teams understand the architecture and decisions behind what they’ve built, along with the methods used to train and operate it, so they can run and improve their AI independently.

At ABN AMRO, we believe that open and transparent AI ecosystems are essential for driving innovation responsibly within the financial sector. Developments such as Mistral Large 4 demonstrate how sovereign and open-weight AI models can expand the range of trusted solutions available to European organizations. We are encouraged by the progress being made and continue to explore how advanced AI can contribute to strengthening critical capabilities, including cybersecurity.

Coen Klaver, Director Cyber Defense at ABN AMRO Bank N.V.

The rapid progress we are seeing in AI models creates exciting opportunities for advanced engineering in chip manufacturing. Our early experience with Mistral Large 4 is promising, particularly for use cases where higher model performance matters. Mistral’s commitment to continued innovation supports our efforts to accelerate the application of AI throughout our semiconductor product lifecycle.

Arnaud Hubaux, Head of AI Program and Strategy.

Mistral Large 4 is an important step forward for financial‑grade AI: an open‑weight model we can fine‑tune to our needs, deploy on our own infrastructure and closely integrate into our digital channels. Hey Belfius is a flagship example of how this partnership helps us rethink how customers interact with their bank.

Nicolas Goosse, Head of Data Insights, Analytics & AI at Belfius

Mastering our AI begins with mastering its architecture and data. For the most sensitive use cases, having access to European open-weight models, which we can deploy on our own infrastructure, is a vital lever for strengthening our strategic autonomy and the resilience of our organizations. The industrial partnership between Crédit Agricole Artificial Intelligence and Mistral addresses these challenges at the Group level. The "Le Chonk" model, which stands out for its reasoning capabilities and performance in the field of cybersecurity, is a promising illustration of the possibilities opened up by this partnership.

Oliver Biton, Group CIO, Crédit Agricole

We're excited about an open-weight model with strong scientific and vision capabilities. Our work is highly specialized, so the ability to adapt a model matters. With Mistral Large 4, we see a foundation for building tools around the way our scientists and engineers actually work with Earth observation data — from imagery to technical documents.

Giuseppe Borghi, Head of ESA Φ-lab

AI sovereignty isn't about choosing which API to call. It's about having the freedom to run, customize, and build AI on your own terms. Mistral Large 4 brings powerful capabilities in coding, multimodal AI, and cybersecurity into the open, giving developers, companies, and countries a great open foundation to build their own AI and defend themselves against cyber threats.

Jeff Boudier, VP Product, Hugging Face

A powerful model is only part of the equation. Developers also need the freedom to decide where it runs, how it is optimized, and how it fits into their systems. We’re excited about Mistral Large 4 because open weights give builders more control over those decisions, rather than making them dependent on a single hosted service. At ZML, we see that freedom as essential to turning advances in AI into useful, deployable software.

Steeve Morin, CEO of ZML

Sovereignty does not always require self-hosting; sometimes it just requires deployments that meet your control requirements. For organizations that prefer a managed service, Mistral Large 4 is available through Microsoft Foundry, with private deployment options for Azure developers.

Microsoft and Mistral AI share a commitment to expanding customer choice in next-generation AI. As the first cloud provider to bring Mistral Large 4 to customers, Microsoft is making Mistral’s latest open-weight model available through Microsoft Foundry, an enterprise AI platform built for evaluating, deploying, and operating models at scale. For organizations advancing sovereign AI strategies, this combination offers greater flexibility and control across their data, infrastructure, and AI operations.

Tina Schuchman, Corporate Vice President, Foundry, Microsoft

Start building with Le Chonk

Mistral Large 4 is available to try, deploy, and customize today.

Get started in Mistral Studio, through the Mistral API, or on OpenRouter. For full control, download the open weights from Hugging Face and deploy on your own infrastructure with vLLM or SGLang. The model card and license have everything you need to get started — and for those who want to go deeper, a full technical report is coming soon.

You can also try the new model in Vibe Code; give it a feature to build or a bug to fix in your own repository.

Mistral Large 4, is also available through NVIDIA-hosted endpoints, as an optimized NVIDIA NIM container for serving with vLLM. Developers can use the open source NeMo AutoModel library for customization or the open source TensorRT LLM library for high-throughput serving.

Enterprises can also tailor Mistral Large 4 to their proprietary data, use cases, and guardrails with Mistral Forge. Talk to our team to learn more.

The model is available to use under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight license, a modified MIT license. The model is free to use, modify, fine-tune, and commercialize, with a single condition: businesses that operate a Model-as-a-Service offering must obtain a separate commercial license from Mistral before using the model commercially.

Starting today, Mistral Large 4 is priced at $0.70 input / M, $0.07 cached input / M, and $2.10 output / M tokens.

We encourage the community to put Mistral Large 4 to the test. Run your own evaluations, push its limits, and share your findings with us on X, Discord, or GitHub.

What's Next

Mistral Large 4 will serve as the foundation for a new generation of specialized and optimized Mistral models. Building on recent releases such as Voxtral and Timestral, we'll continue expanding the frontier of open-weight AI, continuing to give developers and enterprises greater freedom to build, customize, and own their intelligence.

Mistral Large 4

New

Open-weight hybrid instruct-and-reasoning MoE with multimodal input; unifies instruction, reasoning, and agentic capabilities in a single model, state-of-the-art among open weights on cybersecurity, finance, and manufacturing, natively fluent in 160+ languages.

item.title: [Cohere] Build a financial research assistant with Cohere on AWS
item.content:encoded:
Oct 29, 2026

17 minute read

Build a Financial Research Assistant with Cohere AI on AWS

Key takeaways

  • Build a financial research assistant on AWS. Combine Cohere Embed, Rerank, and Parse with Amazon SageMaker AI, OpenSearch Serverless, and Amazon Bedrock to search financial filings and generate answers with page-level citations.
  • Optimize retrieval quality, latency, and cost. Use Embed Pro for high-quality document indexing and Embed Fast for low-latency queries, with configurable embedding dimensions and quantization to balance accuracy and storage.
  • Improve search relevance with Rerank. Reorder retrieved pages using Rerank Pro, and use Context Focus to identify relevant passages and reduce the amount of text sent to the answer model.
  • Handle complex financial documents. Use Cohere Parse for scanned or table-heavy pages, and combine text and page images to help the answer model interpret financial figures and preserve context.
  • Deploy and experiment in your own AWS account. Use the CloudFormation-based demo to explore retrieval, reranking, Context Focus, and citation-backed answers while understanding the tradeoffs of different configurations.

As a financial analyst much of the day comes down to finding one number in a filing that runs to hundreds of pages, and then proving where it came from. Neither is as easy as it sounds. The number is rarely in the body text. It usually lives in a table, a footnote, or a chart, and it can show up in different places under different names.

In this post, we show how to build a research assistant for financial filings with Cohere models on Amazon SageMaker AI - Embed for search, Rerank for ordering the results, and Parse for turning hard pages into clean text. Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock will be used to write the answers, with a citation for every claim.

We will start with what makes this work difficult followed by an overview of the solution, and then spend most of the post on the design decisions behind it and when you would decide differently. At the end, we show how to deploy the solution in your own AWS account and try it yourself.

Why financial research is hard to automate

Financial research looks like a search problem, but it has features that break simple approaches.

The answer lives in the layout. Take a 10-K, the annual report that US public companies file with the Securities and Exchange Commission, covering the business, its risks and its audited financial statements (what a Form 10-K contains). The figure you need from it is usually in a table in the form of net interest income by year, regulatory capital by tier, charge-offs by loan type etc. When a PDF is converted to plain text, tables lose their row and column relationships, multi-column pages can come out in the wrong order, and charts often disappear.

An unverifiable answer is not useful. An analyst cannot put "the CET1 ratio was 11.9%" in a memo without knowing which filing and which page it came from, and whether the figure came from a table, a chart or a sentence. An assistant for this work has to show its sources, and the person reading has to be able to check them quickly.

Volume and cost add up. A research team might index thousands of filings across many years. Every page is embedded once, but every question is embedded too, and every model that runs on every question adds time and cost.

Not every document is clean. Filings arrive as digital PDFs, but also as scanned exhibits, faxed agreements, and photographed pages that have no text layer at all.

Questions do not always come in the document's language. Teams that cover several markets often ask in one language about documents written in another.

So a useful assistant has to do a few things like find the right page when the answer is in a table, make every answer checkable, keep cost and latency under control, cope with pages that are not clean, and work across languages.

**

Solution Overview **

The solution is a research assistant that answers questions about a collection of filings and shows for every claim, the page it came from. It uses four models, each with one job:

  • Cohere Embed turns each page, and each question, into a vector which is a list of numbers that captures its meaning, so that pages about the same thing as the question sit close to it. Embed comes in two tiers: Embed Pro, built for the highest retrieval quality and offline indexing, and Embed Fast, built for low latency on the live request path.
  • Cohere Rerank takes the question and the best candidate pages from the vector search, reads each pair together, and puts them in a better order. With Context Focus, Rerank can also mark the passages on each page that answer the question. Like Embed, Rerank comes in two tiers: Rerank Pro, built for the highest accuracy, and Rerank Fast, built for lower latency. We use Rerank Pro, because for a financial assistant finding the right page usually matters more than a faster answer.
  • Cohere Parse reads a page image and returns a clean Markdown, with tables as real rows and columns. It is used for pages whose text is weak.
  • Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock reads the top pages and writes the answer, citing each page.

People can use it through a web app with three functions:

  • Assistant. Ask a question about the filings. The assistant finds the most relevant pages, reads them, and writes an answer in which every claim cites its page. Each citation also says whether the fact came from a table, a chart, body text, a footnote or a figure, and one click opens the page image to check it.
  • Search. The same search, without a generated answer. It can show the results with and without Rerank side by side, so you can see how reordering changes them, and the Rerank column shows the passage Context Focus picked on each page.
  • Parse. Parse extracts tables as rows from pages that you can download, and scanned-looking pages turned into text.

Under the hood there are two flows. Ingestion runs once per page where Parse runs first, for the pages that need it, then text is embedded with Embed Pro, and the vector is stored into a vector index. Answering runs on every question where Embed Fast embeds the question then the closest pages are retrieved and, optionally, reordered by Rerank. Finally, Claude writes the answer from the top pages. The Cohere models run as real-time endpoints on Amazon SageMaker AI, deployed from AWS Marketplace; the vector index is Amazon OpenSearch Serverless; the web app, sign-in, API and ingestion pipeline are serverless AWS services.

Design decisions, and why we made them

Every one of the challenges forced a choice.

Challenge

What we decided

Why

Answers live in tables

Search on page text that keeps the table markup, and let Claude look at the page image when it writes the answer

Text is cheap to embed and search; the image recovers what the text lost, at the moment a figure is quoted

Answers must be checkable

Cite every claim with its page and where on the page it is (table, chart, text, footnote, figure), and show the page image

The reader can go straight to the source and see what kind of evidence it is

Cost and latency

Index with Embed Pro and query with Embed Fast. Store vectors with 1,024-dimension int8 vectors and make Rerank and Parse optional stages, making the endpoints easy to switch off

Spend on quality once, at indexing; keep every question fast; pay for extra stages only where they help

Pages that are not clean

Route only low-text and table-heavy pages to Parse

Parse is applied where it can change the result, and each page is parsed once

Long pages where only a few lines matter

Send Claude the passages that Rerank's Context Focus picks, together with the page image

Fewer input tokens, the image keeps the context the passages leave out, and the reader sees exactly what the answer used

Questions in other languages

Search all languages in one multilingual embedding space, with no translation step

Eliminates the need for a separate translation step, simplifying the pipeline and avoiding translation-related processing costs.

**Index with Embed Pro, query with Embed Fast

**Indexing and querying have different needs. A page is embedded once, ahead of time, so you can afford the most accurate model. A question is embedded while someone waits, thousands of times a day, so speed and cost per call matter most. Embed Pro and Embed Fast share one embedding space, which means a question embedded with Fast can be compared directly with pages embedded with Pro. You get Pro's quality in the index and Fast's speed on every question, without rebuilding the index. The figure below shows where each model sits.

The second choice is the size of each vector. Embed offers six output sizes, from 256 to 2,048 dimensions, in float, int8 or binary. The embeddings are Matryoshka representations where the model is trained so that the first dimensions carry the most meaning, so a shorter vector keeps most of what a longer one says. We chose 1,024 dimensions stored as int8, one byte per dimension:

  • Storage - A 1,024-dimension int8 vector takes 1 KB of raw storage, compared to 8 KB for a 2,048-dimension float32 vector—an 8x reduction. For a million pages, that translates to approximately 1 GB versus 8 GB of raw vector data. Actual vector index storage and costs will also depend on indexing structures, metadata, and infrastructure overhead.
  • Quality - 1,024 is the middle of the range, and int8 keeps far more detail than binary. That is a sensible default when the answer has to be the right page, not just a similar one.
  • When to change it - Use 2,048 dimensions if retrieval quality matters more than storage. Use 512, 256 or binary vectors for very large archives where cost dominates; binary is 32 times smaller than float32.

Whatever you choose, the query side must use the same size and format as the index. Changing it later means embedding every page again, so it is worth settling early.

**Embed the page text, and keep the image for the answer

**Embed can embed a page's text, the page as an image, or both together as one vector, all in the same space. Each choice suits a different kind of document.

Page text is the cheapest and simplest: one vector per page, Rerank reads text, so it can work on the same pages, and you can show a text snippet next to each result. The catch is that it is only as good as the extracted text where most of the time tables can lose their structure, charts disappear, and a scan has no text at all until something reads it.

The page image needs no text extraction. Tables, charts and layout are seen as the page looks, and it works on scans and photographs. It costs more per page, it is harder to show why a page matched, and Rerank still needs text.

Both together (a fused text-and-image vector) gives the search both views of the page, at the cost of the image price and a larger embedding call.

Annual reports and 10-Ks are digital documents with good text, so we embed the page text. What text loses, mostly charts and complex tables, we recover at answer time instead, by letting Claude see the page image. If your pages are mostly scans, slides, diagrams or charts, such as investor presentations, scanned agreements or faxed exhibits, embed the image or both.

**One embedding space for every language

**Embed supports more than 100 languages and a 128K-token context window. A question and a page land in the same space regardless of language, so a French question such as "impact de l'immobilier commercial sur le segment Global Banking de Bank of America" can find the English Bank of America pages directly. Claude then writes the answer in the language of the question and keeps the citations as they are.

We chose this over translating questions into English first. There is no translation step to build, run or pay for, and no risk of a mistranslated term sending the search the wrong way. Rerank Pro is also multilingual, with support for more than 100 languages. As always, check the languages that matter to you on your own documents.

**Make Rerank an optional stage, and make its effect visible

**Vector search is fast because each page is compared with the question through a single number, the distance between two vectors. A reranker works differently where it reads the question and each candidate page together, which lets it weigh details a single vector cannot hold. Rerank Pro reads up to 32K tokens of question and page together, works across more than 100 languages, and handles semi-structured content such as tables and JSON. In this design, vector search returns 30 candidates and Rerank picks the five that go to Claude.

Rerank sits on the query path, so its latency is felt on every question. We still chose Rerank Pro over Rerank Fast, because in financial research a wrong page costs more than a slower answer. If interactive speed matters more for your users, Rerank Fast takes the same requests and returns the same kind of results, so switching between them is a configuration change, not a code change.

That extra reading costs time on every question and an endpoint to run, and how much it helps depends on your documents and your questions. So we made Rerank a stage you can switch on or off, and made its effect visible: the Assistant shows how long each step took, and Search can show the two result lists side by side, with arrows for how each page moved.

When should you turn it on? Look at where the right page lands without it. If it is usually at or near the top, leave Rerank off and keep answers fast. If it often appears lower in the list, or questions are long and specific, Rerank is the usual fix.

Rerank 5 also returns a calibrated relevance score between 0 and 1 for each page, so the same cut-off means the same thing from one question to the next. You can use it to tell the user that no page is a good match, or to trigger another search, instead of answering from weak pages.

**Parse only the pages that need it

**Parse reads a page image and returns Markdown or content blocks, with bounding boxes, and understands tables, forms, diagrams and images. It is a GPU endpoint you pay for by the hour, and a clean digital page already has usable text, so we use it selectively. A router in the ingestion step decides page by page:

  • Pages with very little text go to Parse (a cover, or a scan with no text layer)
  • Pages where most of the text sits inside tables go to Parse
  • All other pages keep their existing text.

The Parse output is saved, so each page is parsed once, however often you rebuild the index. If you need tables as data, for a spreadsheet or a database, Parse is also the way to get them out of the page.

**Let the answer model read the page, and say where each fact came from

**Search runs on page text, but the answer does not have to. For each of the five pages it picks, the query function sends Claude the page image together with the page text, either the full extracted text or only the passages Rerank marked (see the next section), and tells Claude to trust the image where the two disagree. That is what lets an answer come from a chart, or from a table whose structure the text lost.

Claude is also told to answer only from those pages, to say so plainly when they do not contain the answer, and to cite every claim in the form [document page | kind], where the kind is table, chart, text, footnote or figure. The app turns each citation into a numbered link to the page image, shows the kind next to it, and repeats it on the page ("Answer taken from: table"). An analyst can see which page and type of content the assistant cites as supporting a capital figure, and open the original page to verify the information directly.

The tradeoff is additional input tokens and processing time for Claude. Including five page images alongside their text increases token consumption and response latency, depending on image resolution, page content, and the model used. The demo has a switch to leave the images out, so you can see the difference on your own questions.

**Send Claude only the passages that matter

**Even with the right five pages, most of each page is not about the question. A 10-K page can hold a whole table, a page of risk factors or several unrelated notes, and Claude reads, and you pay for, all of it.

Rerank 5 can do more than order pages. With Context Focus turned on, it also returns the passages on each page that match the question, as character ranges with a relevance score. It is a setting on the Rerank request, not a separate model, and it does not change the ranking. In this design, the query function asks Rerank for the passages on the five chosen pages, and sends Claude only those passages, in page order, instead of the full page text.

That has three effects:

  • Fewer input tokens. Claude reads only the relevant part of each page's text, so answers cost less and come back faster.
  • A sharper prompt. With the unrelated text gone, there is less for the answer model to be distracted by.
  • Easier checking. The app highlights the passages in the page text, so the reader sees exactly what the answer was based on, not just which page.

The tradeoff is context. A passage on its own can lose what surrounds it, such as a table's column headings or the year a column refers to. Context Focus is most effective for targeted questions where specific information can be identified and retrieved. Structured content, such as tables and forms, can be more challenging to split into meaningful chunks because important relationships may span multiple sections. For broader tasks, such as summarizing an entire page, providing the full page content generally produces more complete and accurate results. However, Cohere's internal evaluations show that Context Focus retains the vast majority of answer accuracy even when reducing input tokens by 50–75%, demonstrating that the tradeoff between token reduction and accuracy is far from linear.

This is where the page image earns its place, Claude still sees the whole page, so it can read the headings and units the passages left out. If the lowest token count matters most, send the passages without the images; if the figures must be exact, send the passages with the images. Context Focus returns relevant passages as part of the same Rerank request, without requiring a separate model or additional API call.

The demo has a switch for each: Context Focus and Page images. Each answer shows how many tokens went to Claude and highlights the passages that were sent, so you can see the tradeoff on your own questions.

**Make the expensive parts easy to switch off

**The Cohere models run as real-time SageMaker endpoints, and a real-time endpoint bills for every hour it exists, whether or not anyone is asking questions. For a pilot, or a team that works in bursts, idle GPU hours are the largest cost. So the deployment has one setting that removes all the model endpoints while keeping the data, the index and the web app. Turning the models back on later needs no new ingestion. In steady production use, you would add autoscaling and alarms instead.

**Choosing a pipeline for your documents

**Which stages you need depends on your documents. The figure below is the decision guide we use. It has two steps:

  1. Whether to parse the pages before embedding them
  2. Whether to rerank the results

  • Embed + Rerank is a good starting point for clean digital documents when ordering matters more than speed.
  • Embed only is the fastest, when speed matters more than ordering.
  • Parse + Embed (with or without Rerank) is for scans, faxes, photos, and dense tables where exact figures matter.
  • Parse only is for turning tables, forms, and invoices into structured data, not search.

Note: Rerank is not limited to vector search. It can also improve results from keyword-based retrieval methods such as BM25, enabling workflows like Parse + Rerank without requiring embeddings.

Questions to ask about your own documents:

if .....

Then consider

Your documents are digital and have good text

Embed the text; start without Parse

Pages are scans, photographs or faxes

Parse before embedding, or embed the page image

Answers are exact figures in dense tables

Parse those pages, and let the answer model read the page image

Pages are mostly charts, slides or diagrams

Embed the page image, alone or with the text; let the answer model read it

Interactive speed matters most

Query with Embed Fast; leave Rerank off

The right page often appears low in the results

Add Rerank

Pages are long, or the cost of input tokens matters

Turn on Rerank with Context Focus, and send the answer model the passages

Users ask in several languages

Use the multilingual embeddings directly; no translation step

Whatever you choose, test it on your own documents and questions. A public benchmark tells you how a model behaves on that benchmark's pages, not on your filings, scans or company specific style guides.

Beyond financial filings

The pipeline is not specific to banks. The input is a set of page images and their text, so a different set of documents gives you a different assistant. The same pattern applies wherever answers sit in tables, forms and layouts:

  • Insurance: policy documents, claims and forms, where Parse's structured output can feed downstream systems.
  • Legal: contracts, case files and regulatory material, where clause lookup needs page-level citations.
  • Manufacturing and energy: technical manuals and compliance documents with diagrams and tables, where embedding or reading the page image keeps figures usable.
  • Public sector and life sciences: government and regulatory reports, scientific papers.

Try it yourself

We built a demo of this solution that you can deploy into your own AWS account with one AWS CloudFormation template. The template creates the Cohere model endpoints, the vector index, the ingestion pipeline, the API, and the web app with sign-in. The code is on GitHub.

Scope of the demo

The demo is a working starting point, not a production system. It runs on three public annual reports (Bank of America, Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo, fiscal 2024; 928 pages) from the finance subset of the ViDoRe V3 benchmark (paper), which also provides the sample questions in English, French, Spanish, German, Italian and Portuguese.

To keep the demo small and quick to try, we made some choices that differ from the design above:

  • Pre-extracted document text: Pages are indexed using text provided by the benchmark dataset, simplifying deployment. While the architecture supports Cohere Parse for scanned and complex documents, the demo does not include parsing arbitrary uploaded PDFs.
  • Embed Pro for both indexing and querying: The demo uses Embed Pro for document indexing and query embeddings, eliminating the need for a separate Embed Fast endpoint and reducing GPU costs.
  • Rerank Fast instead of Rerank Pro: Rerank Fast runs on smaller GPU instances, avoiding the higher GPU requirements and potential capacity constraints of Rerank Pro. Both use the same request and response format, so switching to Rerank Pro requires only a template configuration change.
  • Configurable retrieval and answer generation: Rerank is enabled by default in the Assistant, with switches for Rerank, Context Focus, and page images. Search runs without Rerank by default but allows side-by-side comparisons to evaluate the impact on relevance, latency, and token usage.
  • Minimal GPU infrastructure: The demo uses one ml.g5.xlarge instance per deployed model in us-east-1, with AWS Marketplace model packages configured for that Region.
  • Simplified security and access: The demo includes one user, an OpenSearch collection with public network access protected by a data access policy, and no Bedrock Guardrails. These settings minimize deployment complexity and are intended for evaluation, not production.
  • Fixed document dataset: The demo loads a predefined set of financial filing pages rather than supporting ingestion of user-uploaded PDFs.

Things to consider before deploying in a production environment:

  • Network: use a VPC endpoint and private access for OpenSearch Serverless.
  • Identity: use your identity provider, with per-user or per-team access to documents.
  • Encryption: the data bucket uses a customer-managed AWS KMS key; other stores use AWS-managed or AWS-owned keys.
  • Operations: add monitoring, alarms, endpoint autoscaling and a budget alarm.
  • Query model: add Embed Fast for questions.
  • Reranker: use Rerank Pro.

Deploy it

The README in the GitHub repository walks through the deployment step by step: the Marketplace subscriptions and Bedrock access it needs, deploying the stack, loading the data, and signing in. It also covers the cost and how to clean up. The model endpoints bill every hour they run, so turn them off when you finish.

Key takeaways

Building a financial research assistant requires more than finding relevant documents. It means retrieving the right information, preserving context from tables and figures, and making answers easy to verify. By combining Cohere Embed, Rerank, and Parse with AWS services, this architecture provides a starting point for building research assistants that work with complex financial documents.

The key design considerations are:

  • Start with retrieval quality. Choose an embedding strategy based on your documents and validate retrieval performance before optimizing answer generation.
  • Match the pipeline to your documents. Use text embeddings for clean documents, Parse for complex layouts and scanned pages, and image embeddings when visual information matters.
  • Balance quality, latency, and cost. Use Embed Pro for indexing and Embed Fast for querying, and add Rerank and Parse where they provide value.
  • Send the model only what it needs. Rerank's Context Focus picks the passages that answer the question, and the page image keeps the context around them.
  • Make answers verifiable. Provide page-level citations and access to the original document so analysts can check the supporting evidence.

Learn more

To explore the models, technologies, and performance benchmarks relevant to this solution:

  • Cohere Embed
  • Cohere Rerank
  • Cohere Rerank 5 – Retrieval Quality and Context Focus Benchmarks
  • Cohere Embed 5 – Model Capabilities and Improvements
  • Cohere Documentation
  • Amazon SageMaker AI
  • Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
  • Amazon Bedrock

item.title: [Cohere] Who Gets to Build the Frontier for AIWhy the democratic worl…
item.description: Full title: Who Gets to Build the Frontier for AIWhy the democratic world needs more frontier AI builders and how we intend to compete.
item.content:encoded:
Oct 29, 2026

11 minute read

Who Gets to Build the Frontier for AI

Why the democratic world needs more frontier AI builders and how we intend to compete.

Key takeaways

  • AI will become part of the operating infrastructure of economies, public services, and national defence.
  • Who builds it, under what law, and with what accountability will shape the choices available to every country that adopts it.
  • No country needs to build every part of that infrastructure alone. But the democratic world needs more countries and companies capable of contributing to it.

Today, Cohere announced the initial close of its Series E funding round targeting up to CAD $7 Billion, led by Schwarz Group with participation from new and returning investors including Bell Ventures, Bullhound Capital, Inovia Capital, NVIDIA, and Prosperity7 Ventures, and the Government of Canada. We will use the funds to build something increasingly essential in AI: a frontier company outside the U.S. and China. Our ambition is to build frontier models that compete with the best in the world, a secure platform that lets institutions own the AI they run on, and cyber defenses democracies can rely on. We don’t have to accept a future of AI run by just a few, and we shouldn’t want one.

Within a few years, every hospital in Bavaria, every bank in New York and every agency in Ottawa will run a significant part of its operations on AI. They should be able to choose world-class systems built under laws they trust, using technology they can inspect and adapt, deploy inside their own environments, and on platforms they can depend on to remain available when it matters most. Today, many organizations face an uncomfortable choice: cheap models from China or powerful ones you can’t fully see into or control. The market is already choosing: more than 70 percent of the open-model tokens served through OpenRouter came from Chinese models earlier this year – up from 3 percent fourteen months earlier.

We’re focused on changing that.

The need for choice and control is no longer theoretical. Recent history has shown how technologies behind communications, energy, and national security infrastructure can end up controlled by decisions made elsewhere. Access can change overnight because of commercial decisions, export controls, or geopolitical events, often with few alternatives. Each situation was different, but the lesson is the same: countries need guaranteed access to the technologies that keep them secure, resilient, and competitive. As allied governments take on greater responsibility for their own defense, infrastructure, and technological capabilities, AI belongs on that list.

The case against frontier fatalism

When Canada and Germany launched their Sovereign Technology Alliance in Munich earlier this year, they said they were "choosing to build," and that’s exactly what we intend to embody. Yet a growing consensus holds that the frontier of AI belongs to two countries and a handful of companies, and that everyone else should make peace with renting intelligence from whoever wins. You hear versions of this argument in boardrooms, government agencies, and investment committees across the democratic world, usually from people who mean well. Its advocates call it realism. We call it frontier fatalism.

Taken to its logical conclusion, frontier fatalism is a plan for managed decline. It asks countries to abandon capabilities they spent decades building. After investing in research, talent and innovation, they would wire their economies, public services, and defense infrastructure around technologies they don’t control, can’t meaningfully influence, and may not even be able to access indefinitely. And they would be expected to be grateful for API access.

The fatalists are right about one thing: building at the frontier is difficult. It requires capital, compute and research talent at a scale few organizations can assemble. Where they are wrong is in assuming there is only one way to compete.

There are many frontiers

Much of the confusion in discussing frontier AI models comes from talking about “the frontier” as if it were one thing. But there are the myriad domain frontiers: the best achievable performance on a specific class of valuable problem, from finding software vulnerabilities, to analyzing intelligence across dozens of languages, to running a bank's compliance work. Researchers at Harvard Business School referred to this unevenness as the "jagged technological frontier." In many domains, success depends not only on the model itself, but on the system around it: how context is assembled, how state is tracked, how reasoning is verified, and how outputs are evaluated. That reality creates room for more builders. And there are dimensions of the jagged technological frontier where owning, rather than buying, is crucial to one's sovereignty.

The proof: cybersecurity

Cybersecurity is one of the most important domain frontiers today. Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview demonstrated the potential of advanced models to discover previously unknown vulnerabilities, while Project Glasswing extended that work to operators of critical infrastructure in more than 15 countries. Those advances matter. But they have largely occurred behind closed doors, with access limited to a small group of partners on terms set by a single provider, reflecting the same concentration that defines the broader frontier AI landscape. More importantly, they do not prove that leadership in cyber defense will belong exclusively to whichever company builds the strongest general-purpose model.

AISLE, which will soon join us as Cohere Cyber, offers a different perspective. The company describes vulnerability discovery as a production function with two inputs: intelligence per token and tokens per dollar. In practice, that means model capability is only part of the equation. A well-designed system can use efficient models to explore more possibilities, run more tests, and validate more findings. Raw intelligence matters, but so does the ability to turn that intelligence into results.

The evidence is compelling. In August, curl founder Daniel Stenberg reported that Mythos, OpenAI's Codex Security, and ZeroPath had found nothing further in his codebase. AISLE's system subsequently identified 18 of the 24 vulnerabilities fixed in curl's October release. A specialized cyber platform and a general-purpose model are not directly comparable. But that is precisely the point. Organizations do not deploy models in isolation. They deploy systems, products, and workflows. What ultimately matters is the performance of the complete system.

Cybersecurity also offers something uniquely valuable for AI development: ground truth. Suspected vulnerabilities can be reproduced, validated by maintainers, and tested against proposed fixes. That makes cybersecurity not only a critical domain in its own right, but also an ideal environment for improving the models that power it.

How the frontiers feed each other

It may be expected that a company focused on specific domains would fall behind on general models, but in practice the domain work is one of the best ways to make general models better. Working at a domain frontier means pushing for the best possible results on one kind of valuable problem, whether that takes a specialized model, a general model with the right tools and instructions, or a full system built around several models.

Some of the biggest recent advances in model reasoning have come from reinforcement learning on specific domains where a computer can check the answer, such as whether a proof holds, a test passes or a bug that reproduces. The skills models learn inside these domains transfer beyond the domain itself and into related settings, driving general model improvements alongside domain specific ones.

Working with customers on real-world tasks also shows us where today's models fall short in ways public benchmarks rarely capture and each failure tells us what the next model needs to do better. Customers also tell us which capabilities matter most. Public sector customers usually ask first for strong analysis across many languages and the ability to read images and documents alongside text, the same capabilities a bank, a telecom operator or a hospital needs from an AI agent.

All of those improvements flow back into our general models, and better general models make everything we build on top of them more capable, so a customer in one domain benefits from what we learned in another. That loop is why we build on all of these frontiers at once, and this funding round is designed to speed it up.

Europe has done this before

Whether a challenger can take on entrenched giants this way, with a different approach and allies building alongside it, is a question Europe has answered before. Half a century ago, the answer came from commercial aviation.

In the late 1960s, American manufacturers dominated the jet airliner market. Europe’s national aircraft makers were individually too small to challenge them. Britain’s government pulled its funding from the project that became Airbus in 1969. France and Germany pressed ahead. Airbus did not begin by matching Boeing aircraft for aircraft. It competed through a different design: the A300, the world’s first twin-engine widebody. Commercial success took years. A breakthrough came when Eastern Air Lines, led by former Apollo 8 commander Frank Borman, agreed in 1977 to trial four A300s and subsequently ordered more. A decade later the A320 brought fly-by-wire controls to airliners. In 2025, Airbus delivered 793 aircraft to Boeing's 600.

The lesson is that an apparently settled market can be moved by a serious competitor with patient investment, a differentiated approach, and partners willing to build. Airbus builds jets in Mobile, Alabama, and spends more than $15 billion a year with over 2,000 American suppliers. Its A220 began life as Bombardier's C Series, designed in Quebec. Many of its engines come from CFM International, a fifty-fifty venture between GE and France's Safran whose LEAP engine also powers Boeing's 737 MAX. None of that makes Airbus less European. Competition on the airframe and partnership on the engine made both sides of the Atlantic stronger.

That is the model we have in mind for AI. What we are building is a second option for the democratic world, and the United States benefits from it as much as Canada, Germany, and other allies do. The US frontier should not have to carry the competition with China alone. Building more frontier capability across the democratic world makes the entire alliance stronger.

Two decades of building

The foundation for this ambition already exists. AI has always been an international project, and Canada and Germany have been important contributors. In 2004, when neural networks were out of fashion almost everywhere, the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research backed an AI program led by Geoffrey Hinton that brought him together with Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCun, the three researchers later honored with the Turing Award for deep learning. The Transformer paper, published at Google in 2017, was written by eight researchers with roots in seven countries. One was a University of Toronto undergraduate who went on to co-found Cohere. That same year, Canada became the first country with a national AI strategy, anchored by the Vector Institute, Mila and Amii.

Public investment has continued. Ottawa has committed more than C$5 billion to AI since 2017: about C$742 million for the Pan-Canadian strategy, a C$2.4 billion package in Budget 2024 that included the C$2 billion Sovereign AI Compute Strategy, and at least C$2 billion more in this June's AI for All strategy. It has paid off in innovation and talent. With about half of one percent of the world's population, Canada is home to roughly 10 percent of the world's top AI researchers. Germany has made a parallel bet, committing €5 billion to its national AI strategy since 2018 and growing Cyber Valley in Tübingen into one of Europe's largest AI research collaborations.

Research and talent are the foundation. The next step is building companies that can turn them into frontier capabilities, create opportunities for researchers to build at home, and deliver systems institutions can use. That is what this round is for. Investors, research institutions, infrastructure partners, and customers on both sides of the Atlantic are building with us because they believe the future of AI should be more competitive, not ceded to fatalism. Our Series E is the largest funding round ever raised by a private Canadian company, and it carries two decades of public and private investment into a new chapter.

What we will build

Models at every price point, up to the frontier. The frontier is jagged, and the cost of useful capability is falling fast. We will continue investing in frontier models while also building smaller, more efficient models for tasks that don't require the largest systems available. Customers need both access to advancing capabilities and the flexibility to choose the right model for each job based on performance, cost, latency, and deployment requirements. The goal is not one model for every task. It is a portfolio of capabilities that lets customers deploy AI on their own terms. We will continue working with partners across research, sovereign infrastructure, enterprise deployment, and cloud services to meet the full range of customer needs.

A platform customers control. If models are swappable, the durable asset is the layer that governs an institution's data and workflows, and that layer should belong to the customer. North, our agentic AI platform, is built to be that layer. It runs in a customer's own cloud, data center or air-gapped environment and remains model-agnostic, allowing organizations to use Cohere models alongside others of their choosing. The workflows, data, and controls remain with the customer, and no external provider can switch them off. Reliant AI, which joined us earlier this year, extends North’s capabilities into biopharma and healthcare. We will apply the same approach across additional industries, pairing world-class models with purpose-built products designed for real-world deployment.

Frontier-class cyber defense. Cyber is where the domain-frontier thesis has already been proven, and where dependable access matters most. Through our planned acquisition of AISLE, which identified more than 500 CVEs in its first year, we are building Cohere Cyber: a frontier-class system designed to help defenders find, validate, and remediate vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them. It runs on-premises, behind the firewall, or in fully air-gapped environments, ensuring sensitive source code never leaves the building. Because it operates on models hosted by the customer, no external provider can throttle access or turn it off when it matters most. Most importantly, it is built for defense. Its purpose is to identify and fix weaknesses before they become incidents, putting advanced cyber capabilities in the hands of defenders without meaningfully increasing risk to everyone else.

The next twelve months. We will complete our combination with Aleph Alpha and acquisition of AISLE, launch Cohere Cyber for air-gapped and classified environments, release the next generation of our models, and begin frontier-scale training with allied partners. Each step advances the same strategy: stronger models, better systems around them, and more control for the institutions that rely on both.

Building it together

AI will become part of the operating infrastructure of economies, public services, and national defense. Who builds it, under what law, and with what accountability will shape the choices available to every country that adopts it. No country needs to build every part of that infrastructure alone. But the democratic world needs more countries and companies capable of contributing to it.

Canada and Germany have chosen to build, and so have we. If you are a government, a critical infrastructure operator, a researcher, or an American partner who believes the alliance is stronger when more of its members can build, we want to work with you. The frontier is not reserved for a fixed set of countries or companies. It belongs to those willing to advance it.

  • PartnerFinancial ServicesProduct LaunchPitchBook in North: Private market intelligence for enterprise teamsOct 26, 20262 min read
  • Company NewsConcerning behavior from a popular open-weight AI modelOct 26, 202612 min read

Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Enterprise Article

Published October 29, 2026

11

Kate Soule

katesoule

ibm-granite

Luis A Lastras

GrizleeBer

ibm-granite

Subhajit Chaudhury

subhajit1412

ibm-granite

Abraham Daniels

abedaniels

ibm-granite

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

  • Updated Granite Speech ASR model — multilingual speech-to-text across 10 languages with native punctuation and capitalization, so transcripts are ready for downstream models without a formatting pass.
  • Updated Decision adapter in granitelib-core — featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.
