item.description: Full title: Groundhog Day for AI agents: Prompt caching patterns for using OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Groundhog Day for AI agents: Prompt caching patterns for using OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock

Every time you spin off your agent, it has to re-read its whole life story before performing an action. Here’s how to make it remember without having to feed it the same context again.

In the movie Groundhog Day, Bill Murray’s character re-lives the same February 2 every day. He wakes up to the same song playing on the radio, in the same inn, and the same small town, again and again for what some movie fans estimate to be 34 years.

Nothing he accomplished the day before carries over unless he works it out again from scratch. AI agents live in a version of Groundhog Day. Every time an agent takes a step (calls a tool, reads the result, decides what to do next), it has to send the model its entire story so far to maintain continuity: the tool definitions, the instructions, every previous tool call, and every result. The model only predicts the next token based on the input you provide. It has no internal memory between requests, so it must read all of it again. By turn 20 of a coding session, the model re-reads turns 1–19, and it’s you who pays for every one of those tokens, again and again.

Prompt caching breaks the cycle. The service stores your input prompt (instructions, tools, and content) and reuses it on the next request, at a fraction of the input price.

In this post, I walk you through an agent’s life, from its first turn to when it gets new tools and spawns helpers. Along the way, I show you how prompt caching keeps costs down and keeps agents responsive and consistent.

What an agent sends to its LLM

Before talking about caching, it helps to look at what a typical agent’s first invocation to the large language model (LLM) contains:

  • Tool list – The definitions of every function the agent can call. Changes when you ship a new release.
  • Instructions – The developer prompt: rules, persona, policies, examples. Also changes per release.
  • History – Everything that happened in this session so far: the task, the model’s tool calls, and the tool results (which grows every turn).
  • New turn – The latest tool result or user message (which might be different every time).

What an agent sends to the model, turn after turn if you don’t set up caching:

Figure 1: What an agent sends to the model on every turn

How prompt caching works under the hood

When a model reads a prompt, it first does a write called prefill. During prefill, it processes every input token and builds its key and value vectors (also known as key-value, or KV), which form the model’s working state. This happens before the model writes its first token.

Prompt caching saves that state, which contains the system prompt, tools, content, history, and so on. When a later request starts with the same input tokens (that is, the same text), the prompt caching service loads the saved state instead of computing it again. It then processes only what is new in the next payload to the model. Prompt caching can be implicit, where Amazon Bedrock selects where the reusable prefix ends, or explicit, where your code marks that endpoint using prompt_cache_breakpoint. You can use both approaches together, and we recommend doing so.

Turn 1 compared to turn 2

Figure 2: Turn 1 saves the prompt prefix up to the breakpoint, and turn 2 reuses it and pays full price only for the new question

Implicit or explicit, and why do we need both?

For agentic workloads, implicit caching lets Bedrock choose what to cache as the conversation grows. With explicit caching, you can mark shared content, such as tools and instructions, for reuse across sessions and when spinning up helper agents. You don’t always need both forms of caching, but combining them gives you a reusable starting point while Bedrock manages the growing conversation automatically.

New sessions can also reuse that shared starting point while each conversation builds on its own cached history. In this post, we start with the first turn, then show how to carry cached content through later turns, new tools, and across subagents.

Hello cached world

The first win is to cache the static part of the prompt: the tools and instructions that stay the same across requests. These examples use your existing Amazon Bedrock client, TOOLS, and task. Replace the shortened INSTRUCTIONS string with your real policies and examples. The reusable prefix must reach 1,024 tokens to qualify.

When caching static content, use explicit mode: choose where the saved prefix ends.

KEY = "support-agent:v7:gpt-6-astra"
INSTRUCTIONS = "Your full support policies and examples..."

# Rendered context: [provider context][TOOLS][INSTRUCTIONS] | [task]
# Cache starts at the beginning; the marker below chooses its end.
resp = client.responses.create(
    model="us.openai.gpt-6-astra",
    store=False,  # Response storage; prompt caching still works.
    include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"],
    prompt_cache_key=KEY,
    prompt_cache_options={"mode": "explicit", "ttl": "30m"},
    tools=TOOLS,  # Rendered before instructions; keep order stable.
    input=[
        {
            "role": "developer",
            "content": [{
                "type": "input_text",
                "text": INSTRUCTIONS,
                # Save through this whole block, including TOOLS.
                "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"},
            }],
        },
        # User message is processed but not cached.
        {"role": "user", "content": task},
    ],
)

The prompt_cache_key tells the service which requests are meant to share a cache. We come back to how to use it when we get to reading the cache in new sessions. In one of our tests using explicit caching, the roughly 4,000-token tools-and-instructions prefix wrote 4,120 tokens on the first request and read those 4,120 tokens on later requests. The task (or user request) comes after the cache boundary, so this doesn’t trigger a write to the cache.

Keep in mind that prompt caching works only when you pass exactly the same text. Make sure that the agent’s instructions and tool lists are serialized the same way every time. Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and other forms of tool delivery need to be indexed to make sure they stay consistent. Keep anything that varies, such as the date, the user’s name, or a request ID, after the cached instructions.

As the content grows and varies (different tools and content), use implicit mode to let the service follow the conversation. Here, the first request has no explicit marker. Its latest eligible message is the user’s task, so the automatic breakpoint comes after that task and covers the tools, instructions, and task together. The mode is shown explicitly in the following example for clarity, even though implicit is the default. Setting store=False leaves conversation history in your application. It doesn’t disable caching.

def ask_with_implicit_cache(history):
    return client.responses.create(
        model="us.openai.gpt-6-astra",
        store=False,
        include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"],
        prompt_cache_key=KEY,
        prompt_cache_options={"mode": "implicit", "ttl": "30m"},
        tools=TOOLS,
        input=history,  # Everything gets cached
    )

history = [
    {"role": "developer", "content": INSTRUCTIONS},
    {"role": "user", "content": task},
]
# Automatic endpoint: the end of the user message.
resp = ask_with_implicit_cache(history)

This is useful when the next turn continues the same task. A different task doesn’t match the prefix through the old task, and the implicit write doesn’t necessarily create a separate entry for only the tools and instructions. Use an explicit marker there when you need that shorter shared prefix to be reusable across tasks.

Use both when the agent needs a shared starting point and a growing history. Start with the marked developer block in the following code example and call the function ask_with_implicit_cache. The request-level mode stays implicit. The block-level marker adds an explicit save point after the instructions. The service can also save through the latest eligible message. This keeps the shared prefix available while the conversation grows.

history = [
    {
        "role": "developer",
        "content": [{
            "type": "input_text",
            "text": INSTRUCTIONS,
            "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"}, 
        }],
    },
    {"role": "user", "content": task},
]
# Still implicit mode, now with an explicit startup save point in the history.
resp = ask_with_implicit_cache(history)

Caching conversation history and tool results

The model requests tools by name and supplies their arguments. Your application must execute them. execute_function is a helper you build to route those requests to the matching Python functions and return their results. The following loop uses this helper to run each requested tool. It appends the model’s output and all tool results to the history list, then sends that list again until the model returns a final answer. In implicit mode, Amazon Bedrock can reuse the unchanged prefix and cache the added content through the last tool result. Keep earlier messages and the initial TOOLS unchanged.

import json

# Map tool names to their Python implementations.
TOOL_HANDLERS = {
    "get_owner": get_owner,
    # Register your other initial tools here.
}

def execute_function(name, arguments):
    """Run the requested tool and return its result."""
    handler = TOOL_HANDLERS.get(name)
    if handler is None:
        return {"error": f"Unknown tool: {name}"}
    return handler(**arguments)

while True:
    # Preserve all output items, including encrypted reasoning.
    history.extend(resp.output)
    calls = [x for x in resp.output if x.type == "function_call"]
    if not calls:
        break
    for call in calls:
        result = execute_function(call.name, json.loads(call.arguments))
        history.append({
            "type": "function_call_output",
            "call_id": call.call_id,
            "output": json.dumps(result),
        })
    # The last result in this group supplies the automatic endpoint.
    resp = ask_with_implicit_cache(history)

For follow-ups, append a new user message and call the helper again. Keep earlier messages unchanged so their cached endpoints remain available.

Rolling breakpoints: Each turn reads everything before it

Figure 3: Rolling breakpoints, where each turn reads everything before it and writes only its own tool result

For a separate explicit-only run, recreate the two-message history from the combined Hello cached world example. This loop wraps tool results in input_text blocks and marks the final result in each batch. Earlier markers stay in history. See the current lookup rules for long conversations.

import json

while True:
    resp = client.responses.create(
        model="us.openai.gpt-6-astra", store=False,
        include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"],
        tools=TOOLS, prompt_cache_key=KEY, input=history,
        prompt_cache_options={"mode": "explicit", "ttl": "30m"},
    )
    d = resp.usage.input_tokens_details
    print("read", d.cached_tokens, "write", d.cache_write_tokens)
    history.extend(resp.output)  # Includes encrypted reasoning.
    calls = [x for x in resp.output if x.type == "function_call"]
    if not calls:
        break
    batch = []
    for call in calls:
        result = execute_function(call.name, json.loads(call.arguments))
        batch.append({
            "type": "function_call_output", "call_id": call.call_id,
            "output": [{"type": "input_text", "text": json.dumps(result)}],
        })
    # Add the newest boundary; retain every earlier marker.
    batch[-1]["output"][-1]["prompt_cache_breakpoint"] = {"mode": "explicit"}
    history.extend(batch)

GPT-6 Astra tied for the best implicit result in this six-turn workload: about 62 percent lower input cost than running without caching. Explicit rolling breakpoints saved about 61 percent on the same model. Both reused more history as the conversation grew. These are workload results. Measure your own agent’s savings.

Figure 4: Input cost of every caching setup on GPT-6 Astra, relative to no caching

Watch out for:

  • Only a static breakpoint in explicit-only mode – The tools and instructions are cached, but the growing history is processed again on every turn (0.61). This limitation doesn’t apply to the combined example, which also saves through eligible conversation endings.
  • Moving a single breakpoint can prevent cache reuse and cause repeated writes in explicit-only mode. Keep the previous turn’s breakpoint too.
  • Only an implicit write through a changing task – A new task might share the tools and instructions but not the previously saved endpoint. Add an explicit marker after the shared instructions if different tasks need to reuse that shorter prefix.

When tools change

Sometimes an agent’s tool list changes, or new tools get added. Keep the initial list stable: adding, removing, or reordering definitions can invalidate the cached prefix. Choose the approach that fits how the tool becomes available.

When known tools are invoked in different steps of the agent’s flow: Send the same sorted TOOLS and use allowed_tools to limit what the model can call. With allowed_tools, "mode": "auto" lets the model decide whether to call an allowed tool, and "mode": "required" requires at least one allowed tool call. Pass this as tool_choice. The restriction doesn’t change the cached catalog:

tool_choice={"type": "allowed_tools", "mode": "auto",
             "tools": [{"type": "function", "name": "get_owner"}]}

New tools during a session. Both Amazon Bedrock Runtime and Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoints accept an input item type called additional_tools for GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-5.6 Luna. For model availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock. Register the new tool get_due_date in the helper function execute_function, then append its schema to the completed history from the agent loop. Keep the initial TOOLS unchanged:

TOOL_HANDLERS["get_due_date"] = get_due_date
NEW_TOOL = {
    "type": "function", "name": "get_due_date",
    "description": "Return the due date for a support case.",
    "strict": True,
    "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"case_id": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["case_id"], "additionalProperties": False,
    },
}
history.append({
    "type": "additional_tools", "role": "developer",
    "tools": [NEW_TOOL],
})
history.append({
    "role": "user", "content": "Find the due date for case C-123.",
})
# Implicit mode saves through this new user message, including NEW_TOOL.
resp = ask_with_implicit_cache(history)
d = resp.usage.input_tokens_details
print("old prefix read", d.cached_tokens, "new write", d.cache_write_tokens)

# Example output:
# old prefix read 2048 new write 256

A new tool arrives mid-session

Figure 5: Appending a tool keeps the earlier prefix reusable, with example counts from GPT-6 Astra on Amazon Bedrock Runtime

Continue the tool-execution loop with the new response. The loop adds the model’s output to history, runs any requested tools, and appends their results. Keep the additional_tools item in later requests so the new tool remains available. In implicit mode, Amazon Bedrock can cache through the new user message, including the tool definitions that precede it. In explicit-only mode, retain earlier breakpoints and add one to an input_text block in that user message. The additional_tools item itself can’t hold a breakpoint.

Different roles, different catalogs. When different agent roles need different tools, choose a stable tool profile, such as support or billing, at the start of each session. Each profile gets its own cached prefix. Mark the shared instructions so later tasks with that profile can reuse them, then use either mode as the conversation grows.

Cached tool profiles

Figure 6: Each tool profile has its own cached prefix, reusable by matching sessions

Subagents and side calls

Delegating shouldn’t make every helper reread the same background. Share the prefix, then add each helper’s task at the end. Be aware that when you use caching with AI agents, tools and system prompts can be leaked or exploited. Establish responsible AI practices that include your prompt caching implementation as part of that governance.

Warm once, then fan out. Send an ordinary request first and wait for it to finish before launching helpers. Mark the shared context explicitly in every request, even when the mode is implicit:

shared = {"role": "developer", "content": [{
    "type": "input_text", "text": INSTRUCTIONS,
    "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"},
}]}
warm = client.responses.create(
    model="us.openai.gpt-6-astra", store=False,
    tools=TOOLS, prompt_cache_key=KEY,
    prompt_cache_options={"mode": "implicit", "ttl": "30m"},
    max_output_tokens=16,
    input=[shared, {"role": "user", "content": "Reply READY."}],
)
d = warm.usage.input_tokens_details
if not (d.cache_write_tokens or d.cached_tokens):
    raise RuntimeError("Shared prefix was not cached.")
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

# helper_tasks contains the task text for each helper.
helper_inputs = [
    [shared, {"role": "user", "content": task}]
    for task in helper_tasks
]
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
    helpers = list(pool.map(ask_with_implicit_cache, helper_inputs))

The helpers use the same TOOLS, model, and KEY as the warm-up. A warm-up that ends at the output cap can still populate the cache. The usage check confirms cache activity before the helpers start.

Subagents: Warm the shared prefix once, then fan out

Figure 7: Warm the shared prefix before launching helpers, and each helper then adds its own task

Give side calls the same beginning. The agent loop builds history by appending every resp.output and its matching tool results, including encrypted reasoning. After the parent finishes, copy that complete list for a summarizer or judge. The same helper keeps the tools, model, and key unchanged:

from copy import deepcopy

# history is the completed history built by the agent loop above.
# Copy it so the helper can add instructions without changing the parent.
helper_history = deepcopy(history)
helper_history.append({
    "role": "developer",
    "content": "Summarize this conversation in one sentence. Do not call tools.",
})
summary = ask_with_implicit_cache(helper_history)
d = summary.usage.input_tokens_details
print("history read", d.cached_tokens, "write", d.cache_write_tokens)
print(summary.output_text)

# Example output (assumed values and conversation):
# history read 4096 write 32
# Case C-123 is due on October 31, 2026.

The helper can reuse the cached portion of history, but the appended developer message doesn’t automatically extend the cache to include the summary instruction. If later requests reuse the same history and instruction, place the instruction in an input_text block with prompt_cache_breakpoint. For a one-time summary, no additional marker is needed.

Pauses, restarts, and the cache key

Pauses. Cached prefixes have a minimum 30-minute time to live (TTL), refreshed by successful reuse, and might remain longer. If a session resumes soon, an ordinary warm-up can refresh the prefix before it expires. Compare that request’s cost with letting the cache expire. For the TTL rules, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation.

New sessions. Keep prompt_cache_key stable for requests that are meant to share a prefix. A session-specific key isolates sessions even when their prompts match. In the following example, switching to a shared key let sessions reuse the prefix.

New sessions reuse the cache only if they share the key

Figure 8: A session-specific key separates cache entries, and a shared key lets matching sessions reuse them

Reuse of existing cache content requires the same model, AWS account, and Region, and an available matching prefix. The following example combines an explicit startup marker with implicit mode. Each session starts with the same instructions and its own task. Both use the same computed key:

import hashlib

def cache_key(app, model, prompt_version, instructions):
    digest = hashlib.sha256(instructions.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
    return f"{app}:{prompt_version}:{model}:{digest}"

KEY = cache_key("support-agent", "us.openai.gpt-6-astra", "v7", INSTRUCTIONS)
prefix = {"role": "developer", "content": [{
    "type": "input_text", "text": INSTRUCTIONS,
    "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"},
}]}
for label, question in [
    ("session A", "Explain the refund policy without calling tools."),
    ("session B", "Explain the escalation policy without calling tools."),
]:
    # A fresh conversation for each session; the startup prefix matches.
    session_history = [prefix, {"role": "user", "content": question}]
    result = ask_with_implicit_cache(session_history)
    d = result.usage.input_tokens_details
    print(label, "read", d.cached_tokens, "write", d.cache_write_tokens)

On a cold start, session 1 writes the shared prefix. Session 2 can read it even though its task can be different. Each task can also be cached implicitly. Check the usage counters: matching keys and markers make reuse possible, but a cache entry still has to be available.

What prompt caching delivers

Cost. For a GPT-6 Astra powered agent with an 8,000-token startup prefix and six turns adding 2,000 tokens each, one-time static caching reduced cost to $0.50, and rolling breakpoints reduced modeled input cost by 64 percent: from $0.87 to $0.32 per session.

Figure 9: Cumulative input cost per session for the support-agent example, using Amazon Bedrock on-demand prices for GPT-6 Astra

How to tell caching is working

Start with response usage. cached_tokens reports input read from the cache, and cache_write_tokens reports input written to it. As the conversation grows, check that later turns reuse earlier history and that new writes reflect the content being added.

For production monitoring on the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint, use the CacheReadInputTokenCount and CacheWriteInputTokenCount metrics in Amazon CloudWatch. Enable model invocation logging when you need individual request records, then query them with Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights. For the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint, record the response usage fields in your application logs. Its Amazon CloudWatch namespace currently has no separate cache counters.

To check costs, filter AWS Cost Explorer to Amazon Bedrock and group by Usage type. Cache reads, cache writes, and uncached input appear as separate entries per model. Exclude output-token entries when calculating their shares of input cost.

A short checklist

  • Keep the reusable prefix stable. Put shared tools and instructions first, then append conversation history and new turns. Changing a timestamp, message, or tool definition prevents reuse beyond that change. A shorter prefix can still be reused if it has its own saved endpoint.
  • Choose boundaries around content you want to reuse. Use implicit caching for growing history, explicit markers for shared prefixes, or both. Explicit-only mode avoids writing disposable suffixes. When extending an explicit-only conversation, retain earlier markers so later requests can find the saved prefixes.
  • Keep the initial tool catalog unchanged. Use allowed_tools to restrict which tools are callable. Append known definitions with additional_tools, or discover them through namespaced client-side tool_search. Choose a stable tool profile when different agent roles need different catalogs.
  • Check prefix size and lifetime. A cacheable prefix must contain at least 1,024 tokens. Cached prefixes remain eligible for reuse for at least 30 minutes after their latest write or successful reuse.
  • Warm shared content before launching helpers. Mark the shared prefix in both the warm-up and helper requests, including when using implicit mode. Finish the warm-up request before starting parallel calls.
  • Keep cache keys stable within each sharing group. Requests intended to reuse a prefix must use the same key. Separate keys can keep cache accounting distinct between customers or users.
  • Measure savings across the workflow. Cache writes cost 1.25 times the normal input rate. Read prices depend on the model. Track write costs alongside read savings, using response usage during development and monitoring and billing data in production.

Waking up on February 3rd

Bill Murray only escapes Groundhog Day once he stops repeating the same mistakes and starts carrying what he learned from one day to the next. Agents get there in a similar, if less romantic, way: by keeping the start of their prompt byte-for-byte stable and using automatic or explicit cache boundaries as the history grows.

In this post, we covered how to cache shared tools and instructions, grow the cache across agent turns, and preserve reuse when adding tools, launching helpers, or starting new sessions. Keep the shared prefix stable and append new information as the workflow progresses. Use implicit caching for growing conversations and explicit breakpoints for shared content. Combine them when you need both, or choose explicit-only mode when a changing suffix is unlikely to be reused. Compare cache reads, writes, total input cost, and latency to find what works best for your agent. To apply these patterns, follow the Amazon Bedrock prompt caching documentation for OpenAI models and check model availability by AWS Region and endpoint. Start with one workflow and measure the savings as your conversations grow.

About the author

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledg…
item.description: Full title: Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK

This post builds enterprise agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). To see why that’s worth building, it helps to start with where ordinary Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) breaks down. Most RAG systems start the same way: they embed the question, fetch the nearest chunks from one index, hand them to a model, and return the answer. One retrieval, one generation. For a large class of questions that’s the right design, and there’s no reason to build anything more complicated.

It fails in a recognizable way. Ask a question whose answer spans two corpora, and a single retrieval returns half of what the model needs, which is worse than returning nothing, because the answer comes back fluent and incomplete. Ask a question where the right source depends on the question, and a single index has no mechanism to choose. Ask a question that needs a second look at the corpus after seeing the first result, and there is nowhere for that second look to happen.

Enterprise agentic retrieval answers all three by putting a reasoning agent in the loop. The agent decides whether to retrieve, which knowledge base to consult, and whether to go back for more before it composes an answer. This is the direction Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases have evolved. With the launch of the Managed Knowledge Base, retrieval is no longer a single embed-and-fetch call. It has become an agentic capability: multi-turn planning, tool-driven retrieval, and grounded, cited answers. The AgenticRetrieveStream API offers this as a first-class service feature rather than something you assemble yourself. That works, and it also introduces a genuinely harder operational problem. A single-shot pipeline is a function you can reason about by reading it. An agent that reasons and retrieves in a loop takes a different path on every question. By default you can see neither the path it took nor whether the answer it produced was any good. Observability stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the only way to know the system works.

In August 2024, Build an end-to-end RAG solution using Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock and the AWS CDK deployed the single-shot design as a CDK application: an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) corpus, an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection and index, a knowledge base, and a data source, provisioned as CDK stacks whose order you sequenced by hand. Three things have changed since it was published.

  • Amazon Bedrock now offers a managed knowledge base (Type: MANAGED), which owns the ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval itself. The OpenSearch Serverless collection and index that post provisions are no longer something you need to create, scale, or pay for with OpenSearch Compute Units (OCUs).
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides the agentic half, a Gateway that exposes each knowledge base as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool, a Runtime that hosts the reasoning agent, and AgenticRetrieveStream, which reranks internally and returns a synthesized, cited answer. Agentic retrieval is available only on the Managed Knowledge Base.
  • The observability and evaluation story is now something you can provision, not something you bolt on. This solution ships two Amazon CloudWatch dashboards spanning seven layers of telemetry, plus two forms of evaluation, on-demand and continuous, from the same deployment.

This post builds that system: an agent that routes across two knowledge bases, retrieves through the Gateway, and returns a grounded, cited answer, with every layer of its behavior instrumented, as a single AWS CDK application in Python. One command deploys all of it, and CDK derives the order.

If you read the 2024 post, the path from an Amazon S3 bucket to the knowledge base will look familiar, and everything after it is new: the vector store is gone, the retrieval is agentic, and roughly half of what the app provisions exists to tell you what the agent did. If you didn’t, this post stands on its own.

The services at play and the path one question takes through them: the agent decides whether to retrieve and which knowledge base to consult, the Gateway exposes each knowledge base as a tool it can call, the Managed Knowledge Bases search and cite, and the loop repeats as many times as the question needs. Everything the agent does along the way lands in Amazon CloudWatch.

Figure 1: The services involved and the path a single question takes through them

Background

Before the walkthrough, it helps to establish three things: what makes retrieval agentic, why the Managed Knowledge Base is the right foundation for it, and why observability and evaluation belong in the design rather than bolted on later.

From RAG to enterprise agentic retrieval

Classic Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) does one retrieval and one generation. Enterprise agentic retrieval puts a reasoning agent in the loop: it decides whether and what to retrieve, can retrieve several times to refine, chooses which knowledge base is relevant (semantic routing), and only then composes a grounded answer with citations. With the Managed Knowledge Base, this is a first-class service capability, the AgenticRetrieveStream API performs the multi-turn planning, executes the retrieval, and returns a cited answer, rather than an orchestration layer you build and maintain over a raw vector search. That produces better answers on complex questions, but it also produces a more complex system to operate, which is exactly why observability and evaluation are built in from the start.

Managed compared to do-it-yourself Knowledge Bases

Amazon Bedrock now offers a Managed Knowledge Base (Type: MANAGED): Amazon Bedrock manages the ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you, including embedding and reranking with service-managed models by default, so there is no vector database to provision, scale, or patch. This differs from a Customer-managed (DIY) Knowledge Base, where you choose and operate the vector store (for example, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless) yourself.

Two differences matter most for this solution:

CapabilityAmazon Bedrock managedCustomer-managed (DIY)
Agentic retrieval (AgenticRetrieveStream)✅ Supported❌ Not supported
AgentCore Gateway integration✅ Supported❌ Not supported
Data storeAuto scaling, fully managed by Amazon BedrockYou provision, scale, and maintain it
Embedding + rerankingBuilt-in managed models, no extra costYou configure them
Infrastructure to manageNoneVector DB + more

Because agentic retrieval and the AgentCore Gateway connector are available only on the managed knowledge base, it is the natural foundation for enterprise agentic retrieval. It also means Amazon Bedrock manages the storage and indexing for you, so there is no OpenSearch Serverless collection or OCU capacity to provision in this design. The customer-managed option remains the right choice when you want to select and operate your own vector store, for example to reuse an existing OpenSearch Serverless collection or to meet specific data-residency, tuning, or compliance requirements. For enterprise agentic retrieval, the managed knowledge base is what makes the capability possible.

Why observability and evaluation

An agentic system that returns an answer isn’t enough for production. You need to see how it behaves (latency, call volume, token usage), how good the retrieval and answers are, and you need those signals continuously. This solution ships two CloudWatch dashboards spanning seven layers of telemetry, plus two forms of evaluation (on-demand and continuous), all provisioned by the same CDK application. The grounding, citations, and evaluation layers also support responsible use. Cited answers trace back to their source passages so responses stay auditable, and the faithfulness and correctness scores let you catch answers drifting from their sources rather than finding out in production.

Why CDK for this particular solution

Any infrastructure-as-code tool can create these resources. CDK earns its place here for a reason specific to this architecture: the four stacks are densely cross-referenced. The Gateway needs both knowledge base ids. The agent needs the URL and ARN for the Gateway. The dashboards need the KB ids, the Gateway ARN, and the agent runtime id, seven values crossing stack boundaries, each one a dimension on a metric or a target on a connector.

Written as raw templates, that is a set of stack exports and cross-stack lookups kept in agreement by hand, plus a script that deploys in the right order and threads outputs forward, and both drift the moment anything is renamed. In CDK you pass the construct, and the export and the dependency edge are derived from that one act of passing it. The 2024 solution had three stacks and a mostly linear dependency chain. At four stacks with seven values crossing between them, the difference stops being stylistic.

Solution overview

Here is the path a single question takes through the system, end to end. It’s worth a slow look, because the rest of the post walks through it left to right.

The following diagram traces the end-to-end agentic retrieval workflow. A user’s question enters the agent on the AgentCore Runtime, which routes it through the AgentCore Gateway to one of two AgenticRetrieveStream tools, one per managed knowledge base, financial and weather, each ingested from Amazon S3. The selected tool returns a grounded, cited answer, and every step streams to Amazon CloudWatch and AWS X-Ray. The numbered badges map to the following walkthrough.

Figure 2: End-to-end agentic retrieval workflow for a single question

The numbered steps in the diagram map to the workflow, which is as follows.

Step 0 — one-time, at deploy. Before any question is asked, each corpus in Amazon S3 is ingested into its own Managed Knowledge Base: Amazon Bedrock parses, chunks, embeds, and indexes it automatically. This happens once when the stacks deploy, it isn’t part of the per-question path, so it is drawn as a dashed arrow and marked step 0. Every question then follows steps 1–6:

  • A user sends a question to the agent hosted on the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. The Runtime auto-instruments the whole reason-and-act loop with OpenTelemetry (OTEL) spans, so the system is observable from the very first call.
  • The agent’s reasoning model plans and routes across knowledge bases. Because each knowledge base is exposed as its own retrieval tool, the agent selects the tool whose topic matches the question, financial or weather, rather than searching one blended index.
  • The selected tool call is brokered by the AgentCore Gateway over MCP, authorized by the agent’s IAM task role and signed with SigV4, which invokes that knowledge base’s AgenticRetrieveStream API on the Managed Knowledge Base.
  • AgenticRetrieveStream does the within-knowledge-base work: it decomposes the question into sub-queries, retrieves iteratively from the data store that Amazon Bedrock manages (ingested from the corpora in Amazon S3), and synthesizes a grounded, cited answer that streams back through the Gateway.
  • The agent checks whether the returned context is sufficient. If not, it loops, routing and retrieving again, before composing its final answer. If so, it returns the cited answer to the user.
  • Throughout, the Runtime emits spans, token counts, and metrics to Amazon CloudWatch and AWS X-Ray, populating the seven observability layers and feeding both the on-demand and continuous evaluation scores.

Internally, that workflow is one CDK app, app.py, that declares four stacks. You don’t choose the order, CDK derives it from the construct references you pass:

kb_stack = KnowledgeBasesStack(app, f"{project}-kb", env=env)

gateway_stack = AgenticGatewayStack(
    app, f"{project}-gateway", env=env,
    financial_kb=kb_stack.financial_kb,  # ← the reference creates the dependency
    weather_kb=kb_stack.weather_kb,
)

agent_stack = AgentRuntimeStack(
    app, f"{project}-agent", env=env,
    gateway=gateway_stack.gateway,
)

DashboardsStack(
    app, f"{project}-dashboards", env=env,
    financial_kb=kb_stack.financial_kb,
    weather_kb=kb_stack.weather_kb,
    gateway=gateway_stack.gateway,
    agent_runtime=agent_stack.agent_runtime,
)

That is the whole wiring. Those four constructor calls are what replace the export/import bookkeeping and the deploy script.

#StackWhat it createsNote
1-kbS3 bucket, corpora upload, two Type: MANAGED KBs, data sources, IAM, ingestionKBs reach ACTIVE, corpora ingested
2-gatewayGateway (AWS_IAM / MCP), per-KB AgenticRetrieveStream targetsno Cognito needed
3-agentECR, CodeBuild, instrumented Strands agent on Runtime, vended logs/traces, online eval~8–10 min (image build)
4-dashboardsagentic-observability + kb-observability dashboardsempty until you drive traffic

The agent runs a reason-and-act loop: it thinks (a large language model (LLM) call), decides which KB tool to call, reads what came back through the Gateway, and often retrieves again before composing its final, cited answer. Every step is auto-instrumented by the Runtime, so the seven observability layers fill from real traffic.

The seven layers. L1 KB-native metrics, L2 ingestion, L3 agentic retrieval quality, L4 Gateway/MCP metrics, L5 OTEL span tree , L6 token usage, and L7 evaluation scores. Layers 1, 4, and 5 are emitted automatically. Layers 3, 6, and 7 are published as custom metrics by the driver notebook.

Everything tunable lives in one file, config.py:

SettingMeaningDefault
EnvSettings.PROJECT_NAMEName prefix for every stack and resourcebmkb-obs-cdk
EnvSettings.ACCOUNT_REGIONAWS Region to deploy intous-west-2 (or your profile’s)
KbConfig.EMBEDDING_MODEL_TYPEMANAGED (bundled) or CUSTOM (bring your own ARN)MANAGED
AgentConfig.MODEL_IDThe agent’s reasoning model, the Layer 6 spendClaude Haiku 4.5
EvalConfig.SAMPLING_PERCENTAGEOnline-evaluation sampling rate, see the disclaimer100

Changing PROJECT_NAME gives you an independently-named copy of the whole solution, so two deployments can coexist in one account. The driver notebook reads the same constant, so it follows the rename automatically, there are no stack names to keep in sync by hand.

Describe the dataset

The solution ships with two small corpora, bundled in the repository under data/:

  • Financial — A synthetic Octank Financial 10-K (octank_financial_10K.pdf, ~198 KB).
  • Weather — A real, publicly available U.S. Congressional Research Service report on tornadoes (IF12695, tornadoes_report.pdf, ~560 KB).

⚠️ About the data: The financial corpus is synthetic. Octank is a fictional company and the 10-K is model-generated sample data (CC0-licensed). It isn’t real financial data. The weather corpus is a real, public-domain U.S. Government work and is a Congressional Research Service report, publicly available at sgp.fas.org/crs/misc/IF12695.pdf (works of the U.S. Government aren’t subject to copyright). To use your own data, drop files under data/ and adjust the prefixes in config.py, no other change is required.

The two corpora are intentionally distinct, so the agent must route each question to the right knowledge base, the semantic-routing story. Because these are Managed Knowledge Bases, we don’t configure chunking, embedding, or an index: on ingestion, Amazon Bedrock parses each PDF, chunks it, embeds it with its managed model, and indexes it automatically.

We use two separate knowledge bases, each exposed through the Gateway as its own retrieval tool, rather than one knowledge base holding both corpora and that choice is deliberate. Giving the agent two named tools makes routing an explicit act of reasoning it can be observed making: the span tree shows which tool it chose for a given question, and the retrieval-quality metrics in Layer 3 stay separable per knowledge base, so financial and weather precision never blur into a single number. A single tool spanning both corpora would collapse that distinction, the routing decision would move inside one index’s ranking, out of view, and every quality signal would be an average across two unrelated domains. Keeping the corpora and their tools separate is what makes the agent’s behavior legible, which is the whole point of the exercise.

In CDK, getting the corpora into S3 is a BucketDeployment:

s3deploy.BucketDeployment(
    self, "FinancialCorpus",
    sources=[s3deploy.Source.asset(str(ROOT / "data" / "financial"))],
    destination_bucket=self.source_bucket,
    destination_key_prefix=KbConfig.FINANCIAL_PREFIX,
)

BucketDeployment is worth knowing about precisely because the alternative is so tempting: without it, the custom resource that triggers ingestion tends to grow an upload step, and now one resource owns two unrelated jobs. Here it only has to ingest.

Managed ingestion scans, chunks, embeds, and indexes each document automatically: one document indexed per knowledge base, zero failures.

Figure 3: Managed ingestion results, one document indexed per knowledge base with zero failures

Deploy the solution

This section walks through deploying the whole solution with one command. After the prerequisites are met, cdk deploy --all provisions all four stacks in CDK’s derived dependency order and threads every cross-stack value through automatically.

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with permissions for Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore (Runtime + Gateway), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), CloudWatch, AWS X-Ray, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), AWS CodeBuild, Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, and AWS CloudFormation.
  • The agent’s model available in the account (default us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0).
  • CloudWatch Transaction Search enabled, so OTEL spans land in aws/spans for Layers 5–7.
  • Node.js 18+ and the CDK CLI (npm install -g aws-cdk), plus Python 3.13+.
  • The account and region bootstrapped for CDK (cdk bootstrap), once per account/region.
  • No local Docker, the agent image is built by CodeBuild (ARM64).

One command

To deploy the solution, clone the repository, create a virtual environment, install the dependencies, and run cdk deploy --all. Run the following commands from your terminal:

git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/amazon-bedrock-samples.git
cd rag/managed-knowledge-bases/07-IaaC/managed-kb-observability-cdk/
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cdk bootstrap  # once per account/region
cdk deploy --all

The first two commands clone the sample and move into the project directory. The next two create and activate a Python virtual environment and install the CDK app’s dependencies. cdk bootstrap prepares the account and region for CDK (you only need it once per account/region), and cdk deploy --all provisions all four stacks.

Account and region come from your AWS profile (CDK_DEFAULT_ACCOUNT / CDK_DEFAULT_REGION), so the app deploys with no edits.

Region availability: The managed knowledge base, agentic retrieval (AgenticRetrieveStream), and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (Runtime and Gateway) aren’t available in every AWS Region. Before you deploy, confirm that all of these are offered in your target Region, and set ACCOUNT_REGION in config.py accordingly. The default is us-west-2. For current availability, see the Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and the AWS Regional Services List.

There is no deploy script in this version, and that is the point: cdk deploy --all walks the dependency graph it derived from app.py, deploys the four stacks in order, and passes every cross-stack value automatically. The terminal reports each stack as it completes, bmkb-obs-cdk-kb [1/4] (the default PROJECT_NAME), then gateway [2/4], then agent [3/4], then dashboards [4/4] and that order is derived, not declared: it falls out of the construct references between the stacks, so adding a fifth stack that consumes an existing output reorders the deploy on its own.

Stack -agent builds the agent container with CodeBuild, so allow roughly 8–10 minutes for that stage. The other three are quick. Each stack prints its outputs on completion, which is where you pick up the knowledge base ids, the Gateway URL, the runtime ARN, and both dashboard URLs. When the deploy finishes, all four stacks are complete. The following screenshot shows the AWS CloudFormation console after a successful cdk deploy --all.

Figure 4: AWS CloudFormation console after a successful deploy, with all four stacks CREATE_COMPLETE

On the console, all four stacks, kb, gateway, agent, and dashboards, report CREATE_COMPLETE, each with its [n/4] position in the derived dependency order shown in its description.

A note on long-running resources

Two things in this solution take far longer than the 15-minute ceiling of an AWS Lambda function allows for naive polling: the KB ingestion sync and the CodeBuild image build. The AWS CDK Provider framework handles this with an on_event / is_complete split, where one handler starts the work and a second is polled until it reports done.

cr.Provider(
    self, "IngestSyncProvider",
    on_event_handler=on_event,        # StartIngestionJob, return the job id
    is_complete_handler=is_complete,  # GetIngestionJob, report IsComplete
    query_interval=Duration.seconds(30),
    total_timeout=Duration.minutes(30),
)

Nothing blocks, the response protocol back to CloudFormation is owned by the framework rather than hand-written into each handler, and the 30-minute budget is a property rather than something to engineer around.

Launch and test

Open notebooks/01-drive-and-observe.ipynb and run it top to bottom (pip install -r requirements-notebook.txt first). It reads the stack outputs, then sends topic-specific prompts to the deployed agent, one session per KB, so you can see both the answers and the semantic routing in one place: financial questions are answered from the Octank 10-K and weather questions from the tornadoes report, each routed to the matching AgenticRetrieveStream tool automatically.

The notebook discovers everything from the stack outputs, so there is nothing to paste in by hand:

# Stack names are derived from the same PROJECT_NAME the CDK app uses, so renaming the
# project in config.py cannot leave this notebook pointing at stale stacks.
from config import EnvSettings

PROJECT = EnvSettings.PROJECT_NAME
STACKS = {suffix: f'{PROJECT}-{suffix}'
          for suffix in ('kb', 'gateway', 'agent', 'dashboards')}

def outputs(stack_name):
    s = cfn.describe_stacks(StackName=stack_name)['Stacks'][0]
    return {o['OutputKey']: o['OutputValue'] for o in s.get('Outputs', [])}

The notebook imports the same config.py the app does, so the two can never disagree about what the stacks are called.

The driver sends per-KB prompts through the deployed agent. Financial questions route to the financial KB and weather questions to the weather KB, each with a grounded, cited answer.

Figure 5: Per-KB prompts routed to the matching knowledge base, each returning a grounded, cited answer

The notebook also computes the reference-free Layer 3 retrieval-quality signals from what the agent actually retrieved and cited, no ground truth, no extra judge, and publishes them to CloudWatch.

Observe: The seven-layer dashboards

The two dashboards are where the seven layers become visible. The stack creates both dashboards, and driving traffic populates them. The following screenshot shows the two dashboards as they appear in the CloudWatch console.

Figure 7: The two dashboards in the CloudWatch console, end-to-end agentic observability and per-KB observability

Both dashboards appear in the CloudWatch console: one for end-to-end agentic observability and one for per-KB observability (BMKB, Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base). The rest of this section walks through what each layer shows.

In this version the dashboards are built from typed objects rather than a JSON string. A metric is a Metric, a widget is a GraphWidget, and the layout is a list of Rows:

cw.GraphWidget(
    title="L4 — Gateway metrics (MCP)",
    width=12, height=6, period=PERIOD, statistic="Sum",
    left=[
        self._gateway_metric("Invocations", gateway_arn, "tools/call Invocations"),
        self._gateway_metric("SystemErrors", gateway_arn, "SystemErrors"),
        self._gateway_metric("UserErrors", gateway_arn, "UserErrors"),
        self._gateway_metric("Throttles", gateway_arn, "Throttles"),
    ],
)

The practical benefit isn’t fewer lines, dashboards_stack.py runs to 400 lines, more than the equivalent DashboardBody JSON would. It is that a misspelled property or an invalid widget combination fails at cdk synth, on your laptop, in about a second. The same mistake inside a DashboardBody string deploys successfully and renders as a broken widget on the AWS Management Console, where you find it by looking at it.

Because a Row accepts any widget, the documentation is part of the layout rather than a wiki page that drifts. Each dashboard interleaves TextWidgets with the graphs:

[cw.TextWidget(width=24, height=7, markdown=self._l3_explainer())],
[
    self._quality_widget("L3 · Financial KB — agentic quality (reference-free, 0–1)", fin_id),
    self._quality_widget("L3 · Weather KB — agentic quality (reference-free, 0–1)", wx_id),
],

_l3_explainer() returns a markdown table defining each ratio and how to read it, so the widget that explains grounded_coverage ships in the same commit as the widget that plots it, and a reader who opens the dashboard cold doesn’t need to guess what a reference-free metric is.

Dashboard A — agentic observability (end to end). The board opens with an explainer of how each layer counts a different thing (for N queries you’ll see ~N agent invocations, ~2N retrievals, ~3N LLM calls, and ~5N Gateway MCP operations, the agentic loop made visible), then shows KB metrics (L1), Gateway metrics and latency (L4), token usage (L6), and because the agent uses AgenticRetrieveStream, which returns a synthesized, cited answer rather than per-chunk scores, the reference-free Layer 3 quality signals, defined inline and plotted per KB.

One dimension detail is worth calling out, because the typed API won’t catch it for you: the AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases namespace expects a prefixed id, knowledge-base/<id>, while the solution’s own BMKB/* namespaces use the bare id. Both are only strings as far as CDK is concerned.

# L1 — AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases wants the prefixed form.
dimensions_map={"Operation": "Retrieve", "KnowledgeBaseId": f"knowledge-base/{kb_id}"}

# BMKB/* — our own namespaces use the bare id.
dimensions_map={"KnowledgeBaseId": kb_id}

Layer 5: The span tree

Layer 5 is the raw OTEL span tree in aws/spans, and it is the layer that shows you the agentic loop directly. It is worth reading carefully, because the nesting isn’t obvious: one LLM call produces three spans. The Strands invoke_agent span wraps the turn, an internal chat span wraps the model call, and a chat <model> span of kind CLIENT is the actual call, and all three repeat the same gen_ai.usage.* token attributes.

The following screenshot shows the span tree in aws/spans, with the three-span nesting visible in the top rows.

Figure 14: Layer 5 span tree in aws/spans, showing the three-span nesting of a single LLM call

Reading the top three rows: an invoke_agent Strands Agents aggregate, then an internal chat span, then a CLIENT chat span, all reporting an identical 7,299 input and 268 output tokens. That is the same LLM call appearing at three levels of the tree, which is why aggregation needs care.

That structure matters the moment you aggregate. To count each LLM call once, filter to the CLIENT leaf:

fields attributes.gen_ai.request.model as model,
       attributes.gen_ai.usage.input_tokens as in_tok,
       attributes.gen_ai.usage.output_tokens as out_tok
| filter ispresent(in_tok) and kind = 'CLIENT' and name like /^chat /
| stats sum(in_tok) as input_tokens, sum(out_tok) as output_tokens,
        count(*) as llm_calls by model

Without that filter the same query reports three times the tokens and three times the calls.

Applying that CLIENT-leaf filter, the following screenshot shows generation token usage by model with each LLM call counted once.

Figure 15: Generation token usage by model, with each LLM call counted once

With the filter in place, the run shows 14 LLM calls totaling 60,472 input and 2,709 output tokens. Without it, the same query would report three times the calls and three times the tokens.

Evaluate: On-demand and continuous

Quality is measured two ways, and both are provisioned by the app.

On-demand: The driver notebook calls AgentCore There is no deploy script in this version, and that is the point: (LLM-as-judge) over each session’s spans for built-in evaluators, Correctness, Faithfulness, Tool-Selection Accuracy and publishes the scores to CloudWatch, where they appear as Layer 7 on Dashboard A.

The following screenshot shows Layer 7 on Dashboard A: on-demand evaluation scores per knowledge base, with the Layer 5 OTEL span table on the same dashboard.

Figure 16: Layer 7 on-demand evaluation scores per knowledge base, beside the Layer 5 span table

Layer 7 shows the on-demand evaluation scores per knowledge base, with the Layer 5 OTEL span table alongside, so the scores and the spans that produced them read together on one board.

Continuous (online): The agent stack also provisions an AWS::BedrockAgentCore::OnlineEvaluationConfig that samples live sessions and scores them automatically, no notebook run required. The configuration itself is visible in the Bedrock AgentCore console under Assess → Evaluations → Evaluation configurations. Results land in the log group /aws/bedrock-agentcore/evaluations/results/<config-id>, and every score is also published as a CloudWatch metric in the Bedrock-AgentCore/Evaluations namespace, keyed by evaluator name and configuration id, so you can graph the scores or alarm on them without parsing logs.

The following screenshot shows the online evaluation configuration in the AgentCore console, under Assess, then Evaluations, then Evaluation configurations.

Figure 17: The online evaluation configuration in the AgentCore console, with four built-in evaluators at 100 percent sampling

The configuration lists four built-in evaluators, Tool-Selection Accuracy, Faithfulness, Correctness, and Response Relevance, set to 100 percent sampling and shown as ACTIVE and enabled.

Because the scores are ordinary CloudWatch metrics, they graph like anything else, no log parsing, and the same widget could carry an alarm. The following screenshot shows those four evaluator scores graphed as ordinary CloudWatch metrics.

Figure 18: The four continuous evaluator scores graphed as ordinary CloudWatch metrics

The four evaluator scores appear as metrics in the Bedrock-AgentCore/Evaluations namespace, each keyed to the evaluation configuration id and the agent’s service name, so you can graph them or alarm on them without parsing logs.

Online results only arrive after a session closes. Scoring runs on the completed session, so the results log group stays empty for roughly the session idle timeout (~30 minutes) after you drive traffic. An empty group right after a run is expected, not a misconfiguration. Each result event carries session.id, so it joins to every other layer. The on-demand path in the notebook has no such wait, which is why both are here.

Across the four built-in evaluators on this run, the continuous path scored 1.00 on Correctness, Faithfulness, Response Relevance, and Tool-Selection Accuracy, five scored traces per evaluator, each result carrying a written explanation.

⚠️ Sampling and cost. This app sets SAMPLING_PERCENTAGE = 100 purely for the blog experiment, so every session is scored and the results are immediately visible. This isn’t a production recommendation. Online evaluation invokes an LLM-as-judge per sampled session, so cost scales with the sampling rate and traffic volume. For a real deployment, choose a sampling percentage that fits your quality-monitoring needs and budget, and align the configuration with your organization’s own policies and cost-governance requirements before enabling it. The rate is a single constant, EvalConfig.SAMPLING_PERCENTAGE, in config.py.

Clean up

When you’re finished, remove the solution so it stops incurring charges, since stored KB data, the agent image in ECR, and the still-active online evaluation all cost money while the stacks sit idle. One command tears everything down:

cdk destroy --all

CDK deletes the stacks in reverse dependency order on its own, dashboards, then agent, then gateway, then kb: the same graph it derived for the deploy, walked backward. There is no teardown script to keep in agreement with the deploy script, which is one of the more quietly valuable properties of modelling the dependencies once.

Two removal behaviors are worth knowing, because both replace hand-written cleanup code:

self.source_bucket = s3.Bucket(
    self, "SourceBucket",
    removal_policy=RemovalPolicy.DESTROY,
    auto_delete_objects=True,  # replaces a list_object_versions delete loop
)

self.repository = ecr.Repository(
    self, "AgentImageRepo",
    removal_policy=RemovalPolicy.DESTROY,
    empty_on_delete=True,  # replaces an image-delete loop
)

Both are set for sample hygiene, for anything you care about, switch the bucket to RemovalPolicy.RETAIN.

The CDK bootstrap stack (CDKToolkit) and its staging bucket aren’t removed. They are shared account-wide infrastructure that other CDK apps may depend on.

What changed since the single-shot solution

Both this post and the 2024 solution are CDK applications in Python, deployed with cdk deploy. The authoring tool is the constant here, what changed is the architecture underneath it, and most of the change is subtraction:

Concern2024: Single-shot RAGThis solution
Vector storeAn OpenSearch Serverless collection and index you provision, scale, and pay OCU forNone. Type: MANAGED, Amazon Bedrock owns storage and indexing
Index lifecycleA custom resource creates the index and waits for it to become searchableNothing to create
Embedding modelYou select it and grant model accessService-managed by default
Stacks3: KB role → OpenSearch infra → KB + data source4: kb → gateway → agent → dashboards
RetrievalOne Retrieve, top-k chunks by vector similarityAgenticRetrieveStream, reranked internally, returns a synthesized cited answer
Choosing a knowledge baseNot applicable, there is one indexThe agent routes semantically across two
Second look at the corpusNot possible in one shotThe agent retrieves again before answering
TelemetryNone provisionedSeven layers, two dashboards
EvaluationManual: sync, pick a model, ask questionsOn-demand and continuous, both provisioned
Cost floor when idleOCU charges accrue whether or not you queryStorage only

The trade is real in both directions. A single index answering single-shot questions is cheaper per query, simpler to reason about, and entirely sufficient when one corpus holds the answer. Reach for this design when it doesn’t.

The CDK constructs doing the work

Four constructs carry most of the weight in this app, and they are worth naming because each replaces something people otherwise hand-write:

  • Provider – For custom resources that outlive the 15-minute ceiling of an AWS Lambda function. The on_event / is_complete split means nothing sleeps in a poll loop, and the response protocol back to CloudFormation is the framework’s job rather than a vendored urllib callback in every handler.
  • BucketDeployment – Uploads the corpora, so the ingestion custom resource only ingests.
  • auto_delete_objects=True and empty_on_delete=True, replace the hand-written list_object_versions and image-delete loops that a stack otherwise needs to be destroyable at all.
  • repository.grant_pull_push(project) – One line for the eight ecr:* actions CodeBuild needs, spelled correctly by construction.

And typed dashboards, from the Observe section: Metric / GraphWidget / Row objects instead of a DashboardBody JSON string, which moves an invalid widget combination from “renders broken on the console” to “fails at cdk synth.”

Two things CDK doesn’t change, and both are worth knowing before you start:

  • Free-form JSON stays camelCase. connector_parameters and parameter_values are passed through verbatim, so the AWS CDK snake_case to PascalCase conversion does not apply inside them. Keys like bucketName and inclusionPrefixes must be spelled exactly as the API expects, and nothing will tell you otherwise until the resource fails.
  • String-typed values are still strings. The knowledge-base/<id> versus bare <id> dimension difference from the Observe section is invisible to the type system. Typed constructs check structure, not semantics.

Neither is a reason to prefer one tool over the other. They are the boundary of what “typed” buys you, and knowing where that boundary sits is most of what makes CDK pleasant instead of surprising.

Conclusion

We built a complete enterprise agentic retrieval solution on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base and AgentCore: multi-KB semantic routing, a reasoning agent, seven layers of observability, and both on-demand and continuous evaluation, and deployed all of it as a single AWS CDK application.

Two things are worth taking away. The managed knowledge base removed infrastructure rather than adding it: no vector store to provision, no index to create and wait on, no OCU line item accruing while the system sits idle. It is also the knowledge base type that supports agentic retrieval and the AgentCore Gateway connector, as described in the Amazon Bedrock documentation. And once retrieval became agentic, observability stopped being optional. Roughly half of what this app provisions exists to answer what the agent actually did and whether the answer was any good, which isn’t overhead on an agentic system. It’s the part that makes one operable.

The CDK authoring model earned its place on the seams. Seven values cross stack boundaries in this architecture, and every one of them is a construct reference rather than an export/import pair, which is also why there’s no deploy script, no teardown script, and no fixed order to remember.

From here you can point the data sources at your own corpora, place the agent in a virtual private cloud (VPC), tune the online-evaluation sampling rate to your budget and policies, or add more knowledge bases to the router. To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock detail page and the Amazon Bedrock documentation. The app, the driver notebook, and the self-contained utilities are all in the accompanying GitHub repository, so you can clone it and deploy your own copy with one command.

About the authors

item.title: [Anyscale] KubeRay in production: best practices from the field
item.content:encoded:
HomeBlogBlog Detail

KubeRay in production: best practices from the field

By Naila Khan | October 26, 2026

Part 2 of our KubeRay series, from the field. Part 1: Running Ray at scale on Kubernetes with KubeRay covers what KubeRay is, its custom resources, and how to deploy your first RayJob.

Part 1 ended on a good moment: a RayJob reaching SUCCEEDED. This post picks up from there, with what changes when that one job becomes hundreds, spread across teams and clusters. KubeRay handles that growth well; a public Ray Summit 2024 talk showed Ray Train scaled to 10,000 Kubernetes nodes.

If you've run Ray on Kubernetes for a while, you may know the moment. Somewhere past a handful of nodes and a second team, a failed GPU job stops being a quick kubectl logs. The cluster that held the answer may already be gone, and the GPUs reserved for the rerun keep billing while someone works out whether it was the code, the data or the hardware.

As a field engineer, I spend a lot of time with two kinds of teams: enterprises fitting Ray into clusters built for something else, and digital natives pushing Ray further than it has been pushed before. They tend to meet the same handful of scenarios, and they've taught me which practices hold up. That's what this post shares.

LinkFrom the quickstart to production

Part 1's example trains Fashion MNIST on CPUs. A production RayJob uses the same resource, with four changes: it requests GPUs, queues behind team quotas through Kueue, keeps work off the head node, and scales workers from zero.

1apiVersion: ray.io/v1
2kind: RayJob
3metadata:
4  name: nightly-train
5  labels:
6    kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: team-ml   # same quotas as every other GPU workload
7spec:
8  entrypoint: python train.py
9  shutdownAfterJobFinishes: true         # GPUs go back to the pool when done
10  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 300
11  rayClusterSpec:
12    enableInTreeAutoscaling: true
13    headGroupSpec:
14      rayStartParams: { num-cpus: "0" }   # keep work off the head node
15      template: { ... }
16    workerGroupSpecs:
17      - groupName: gpu-workers
18        minReplicas: 0
19        maxReplicas: 16
20        template: { ... }                # nvidia.com/gpu requests go here

At this scale, the features from Part 1 do more of the work: GPU nodes shared across jobs, workers that scale back to zero, and quotas that keep teams fair. For one team on one cluster, this spec is often all you need.

Note the shutdownAfterJobFinishes: true line, though. It is good for cost, and it is also where the first production scenario starts.

LinkFive production scenarios to plan for

Once Ray becomes shared infrastructure, with more teams, more clusters and GPUs you can't afford to waste, the same pattern shows up in the field: defaults that work well at small scale need returning under production parallelism and contention. These are not KubeRay issues. Each sits on the boundary between Ray, Kubernetes and the organization running both.

  • Debugging data is tied to the cluster's lifetime. A RayJob that cleans up after itself also deletes its Ray dashboard. The hardest case is a driver that exits in its first few minutes: GPU workers come up, receive no tasks, and the cluster is torn down before anyone captures the driver log. That leaves little to investigate afterward.
  • Hardware faults surface as application errors. A PCIe or NVLink fault, or a hung NFS mount, can interrupt a training run while the pod still reports Ready. Ray continues to schedule work there, so the failure presents as an application error. Some teams have built a modified operator and a custom resource to detect failing hardware.
  • Default settings need tuning at scale. With 20 clusters competing for one GPU pool, an idle GPU worker can be reaped while its placement group is still forming, and training can't begin. A maxReplicas set with no headroom can stall the autoscaler when Ray Train retries an out-of-memory task. Each retry can also leave a placement group behind. Teams in the field report weeks of platform engineering before reliability stabilizes.
  • Head node disruptions affect the whole cluster. Node drains for node-image updates and security patches can take Ray nodes down, and memory pressure can evict the head pod, as Klaviyo's engineering team describes from a year of running Ray Serve on KubeRay. Without GCS fault tolerance, the whole cluster fails. With it, workers keep running only if the head recovers within about ten minutes, KubeRay's default worker reconnect timeout.
  • Ray shares the cluster with existing platform services. Service meshes, shared namespaces, quotas and audit requirements were there first. One enterprise team serving thousands of models on Ray Serve found its Envoy sidecars creating a listener for every Ray port, which strained the mesh control plane and affected neighboring services.

LinkSix best practices for production KubeRay

None of these needs new tooling. Each practice maps to one of the scenarios above and uses what the Kubernetes ecosystem already gives you.

Link1. Persist logs and events before the cluster goes away

Plan for the Ray dashboard of an ephemeral cluster to go away. Turn on the History Server from Part 1 so Ray events and logs land in object storage, and test it against short-lived runs: a driver that crashes in its first minutes is the case teams most often miss. If your team debugs in an existing log stack, also ship logs there with a sidecar such as Fluent Bit. For a job you are actively debugging, raise ttlSecondsAfterFinished so the cluster outlives the failure long enough to inspect.

Some context on why this matters. Seeing logs and dashboards for a finished RayJob is one of the oldest asks in the KubeRay community; users were raising it as early as 2023. It is hard because ephemeral clusters are the whole point of RayJob, so the evidence has to leave the cluster before the cluster does. The History Server is the community's answer, built with contributors from several large platform teams. It was introduced as alpha in KubeRay v1.6 and promoted to beta in v1.7. It writes Ray events and logs to object storage and lets you inspect them after the cluster is deleted.

Link2. Treat GPU health as a scheduling signal

Run NVIDIA's DCGM exporter and alert on GPU Xid errors, not only on utilization. Use node health checks to taint or cordon a failing node so new Ray pods stop landing there. Then use the label-aware scheduling from Part 1 to keep new Ray work on healthy nodes. KubeRay maintainers are also discussing forwarding Kubernetes Pod events, including device-related failures, to RayCluster resources for remediation (issue #5304).

Link3. Tune for contention, not for a quiet cluster

Test your configuration at production parallelism, not on one cluster. Five settings come up repeatedly in the field:

  • Gang scheduling: use one of the gang schedulers from Part 1 (Volcano, YuniKorn, scheduler-plugins or NVIDIA KAI Scheduler) so a job's workers start together or not at all. This stops early workers from sitting idle while a placement group forms.
  • Idle timeout: if you don't gang-schedule, raise the idle timeout so early GPU workers survive while the rest of a placement group forms.
  • maxReplicas headroom: leave room for the replacement worker Ray Train requests after an out-of-memory kill. Size it for your needed workers plus at least two.
  • Bounded retries: cap out-of-memory retries with RAY_task_oom_retries so repeated retries can't run for hours.
  • Mixed CPU and GPU pools: watch whether the autoscaler adds CPU nodes while GPUs are the bottleneck, and whether idle CPU nodes scale down during GPU-bound stages.
1autoscalerOptions:
2  idleTimeoutSeconds: 600   # default is 60
3workerGroupSpecs:
4  - groupName: gpu-workers
5    maxReplicas: 10          # 8 needed + headroom for retries

Watch for placement groups left behind after retries, too. They hold resources the autoscaler can't reclaim.

Link4. Design for losing the head node

  • Set num-cpus: "0" on the head so CPU tasks and actors aren't scheduled there.
  • When you enable GCS fault tolerance, give each critical workload its own external Redis so a Redis issue stays contained to one workload.
  • Bake dependencies into the image instead of installing them at runtime, which can fill ephemeral storage and get pods evicted.
  • For Ray Serve, set max_replicas_per_node so a single node failure affects only part of a deployment.

Link5. Fit Ray into the cluster you already have

  • Give Ray its own namespace, with the RBAC and NetworkPolicy controls from Part 1, so Ray workloads stay isolated from neighboring services.
  • If you run a service mesh, keep it at the edge. Exclude Ray's internal ports from the sidecar, and encrypt Pod-to-Pod traffic with Ray's own TLS or KubeRay's mTLS support (alpha in v1.7) instead. A sidecar listener for every Ray port can overload the mesh.
  • Label every RayJob and RayService with its team and cost center, so the Kueue quotas from Part 1 also give you attribution and chargeback.

Link6. Alert on the failures that matter, and automate the first response

Alert on RayJob Failed status, head pod restarts and GPU Xid errors. Start from what Part 1 covered: KubeRay's Kubernetes-native status fields and Events already report RayJob and RayCluster state, and kubectl ray gives on-call engineers a quick view. Where the response is always the same, such as cordoning a node with a failing GPU, automate it so the on-call engineer starts from an answer instead of a dashboard.

LinkWhen the glue starts to cost you

In Part 1, KubeRay replaced the glue between Ray and Kubernetes. At fleet scale, a new layer of glue appears. Every practice above is doable. Each one is also glue: something a person on your team builds, maintains and supports. With one team on one cluster, that's manageable. It changes with the second team and the second cluster, when a failed job, a three-hour queue wait or an auditor's question each take real time to answer.

A quick self-check. Do you:

  • Maintain a pipeline just to capture logs before ephemeral RayJobs terminate?
  • Spend hours working out whether a failure was the GPU, Kubernetes or Ray?
  • Hand-tune autoscaler defaults to keep production jobs from stalling?
  • Run redundant clusters or a custom health checker to keep Ray Serve up?
  • Map workloads to teams by hand for audit or chargeback?
  • Operate Ray across several clusters, clouds or regions, beyond what MultiKueue covers?

If two or more describe your week, a platform layer is likely worth a look.

LinkWhat comes next: KubeRay Connect

We built Anyscale KubeRay Connect, now in private preview, so teams don't have to keep building that layer themselves. It sits on top of the KubeRay you already run. Your operator keeps reconciling your CRs, you keep submitting with kubectl apply, and your Kueue queues and GitOps stay as they are. Nothing is rewritten.

Whether you're just starting with KubeRay or already running it in production, keep your existing Kubernetes and KubeRay stack and extend your platform with full-stack observability, multi-cloud orchestration, security, governance, and enterprise support, so your developers stay productive and ship faster.

KubeRay Connect installs with a Helm chart as a thin layer beside your workloads. A small Anyscale Connector patches your KubeRay specs at admission and injects lightweight telemetry sidecars. A collector ships metrics and Kubernetes events to the Anyscale platform.

Here is how Connect maps to the five scenarios:

ScenarioWhat KubeRay Connect does
Debugging data is tied to the cluster's lifetimePersisted task and actor dashboards, aggregated logs, and job, service and autoscaler events, managed for you and viewable in the Anyscale console without kubectl access
Hardware faults surface as application errorsCorrelates GPU metrics, Kubernetes events and Ray signals in one place, so a hardware fault appears next to the affected task
Default settings need tuning at scaleShows autoscaler events and GPU utilization per job, so you can see when idle timeouts and replica limits are wrong. Orchestrate adds single-cluster job submission, scheduling and status tracking alongside your Kueue queues. Automated tuning of Ray settings is on the roadmap.
Head node disruptions affect the whole clusterShows the events around a failure; your resilience design stays yours
Ray shares the cluster with existing platform servicesInstalls beside your existing stack: outbound-only connections, no control-plane ingress, and your Kueue queues and GitOps unchanged. Identity passthrough for RBAC and attribution is on the roadmap.

Connect works alongside your cluster design: mesh configuration, Redis topology and image size stay your choice, and the practices above still apply. Mapping identity to people and placing work across a fleet stay with you today, and preview users are shaping what comes next.

The security model is built for review. Every connection starts inside your cluster, so the control plane needs no ingress. Authentication uses projected ServiceAccount OIDC tokens instead of API keys. Admission is fail-closed by default, so a workload is never silently admitted without telemetry.

LinkGet started

KubeRay is a strong foundation, and the six practices above will take you a long way. When you'd rather spend your team's time on models than on glue, a maintained platform layer gives that time back.

  • Running KubeRay in production? Apply for the KubeRay Connect private preview.
  • At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 (November 9–12, Salt Lake City)? Register and come say hello. We'd love to hear about your clusters and what your team is working through.
  • New to KubeRay? Start with Part 1: Running Ray at scale on Kubernetes with KubeRay.
  • Join the community. Share what you've learned in #kuberay on the Ray Slack, or at the bi-weekly KubeRay community meeting.

Table of contents

  • From the quickstart to production
  • Five production scenarios to plan for
  • Six best practices for production KubeRay
  • 1. Persist logs and events before the cluster goes away
  • 2. Treat GPU health as a scheduling signal
  • 3. Tune for contention, not for a quiet cluster
  • 4. Design for losing the head node
  • 5. Fit Ray into the cluster you already have
  • 6. Alert on the failures that matter, and automate the first response
  • When the glue starts to cost you
  • What comes next: KubeRay Connect
  • Get started

Sharing

Sign up for product updates
