It combines a $0.05 blended price, $0.015/M cached input, 100% uptime on OpenRouter’s tracking, and the highest measured output speed. Because reasoning models shift spend toward output tokens, model your real inference costs against your own token ratios before you commit.

Related articles

GLM-5.1 Model Overview: Features, Capabilities & Use Cases<p>GLM-5.1 is Z.AI’s next-generation flagship model for agentic engineering, released on April 7, 2026 under the MIT license. It is a 754-billion parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 40 billion active parameters per token, a 202,752-token context window, and up to 131K output tokens. The model is the direct successor to GLM-5, designed specifically for long-horizon autonomous […]</p>

Best Kimi K3 SaaS Tools & API Platforms<p>Kimi K3, with its 2.8 trillion parameters and 1M-token context window, represents a significant leap in large language model capabilities. However, deploying, accessing, and managing a model of this scale presents real infrastructure challenges. From optimizing inference latency and managing GPU compute costs to handling multimodal vision capabilities, selecting the right deployment platform is critical […]</p>

Best SaaS Tools and API Providers for GLM-5.2<p>GLM-5.2 represents a significant leap forward in open-weight models, particularly for complex reasoning, long-context processing, and agentic coding tasks. Deploying a model of this scale — especially with its massive 1-million token context window and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture — presents real infrastructure challenges. Managing memory bandwidth, optimizing time to first token (TTFT), and handling quantization […]</p>

item.title: [DeepInfra] Wan 3.0: Model Documentation & Integration Guide
item.content:encoded:
Wan 3.0: Model Documentation & Integration Guide

Published on 2026.10.22 by DeepInfra

Wan3.0 is an all-in-one video generation model from Wan-AI, hosted on DeepInfra. It covers reference-based generation, editing, replication, and driving in a single model, and it accepts images, video clips, audio, documents, and web links as input.

Use it for cinematic storytelling, social media content, and video editing. Every generation includes synchronized audio by default, and the model keeps characters stable and recognizable across a clip.

Key Capabilities

  • Omni-modal reference: Parses documents, web pages, and complex images to drive video generation.
  • Long clips with audio: Generates up to 30 seconds of video with a synchronized audio track by default.
  • Character consistency: Keeps subjects stable and recognizable for the full duration of a video.
  • Editing and extension: Handles style transfers such as clay art conversions, and extends existing videos forward or backward.

Technical Specifications and Benchmarks

Standard specifications

MetricSpecificationNotes
Maximum resolution1080P480P, 720P, and 1080P tiers
Frame rate30 fpsOutput is an MP4 video
Duration2 to 30 secondsSet -1 to let the model choose
AudioGenerated by defaultSet audio to false for silent output
Reference inputsImages, video, audio, files, linksUp to 20 reference assets per request

Quality benchmark

Artificial Analysis measures video quality through blind user votes in its Video Arena. Wan3.0 ranks first on both of its text-to-video leaderboards.

LeaderboardEloRank
Text-to-video with audio1,173 (95% interval 1,157 to 1,189)1
Text-to-video without audio1,1341

On the with-audio board, Wan3.0 leads Utopai X at 1,166 and Dreamina Seedance 2.5 at 1,159. The rank interval spans first to third, so the top models sit close together.

Comparison with Wan2.7

FeatureWan2.7Wan3.0
Input typesImage or reference video, depending on the modelText, images, video, audio, files, and web links
Maximum duration15 seconds30 seconds
Models on DeepInfraSeparate image-to-video and reference-to-video modelsOne model for every workflow
Price on DeepInfra$0.10 per second$0.20 per second

Both Wan2.7 models remain available, including Wan2.7 image-to-video. Alibaba introduced video editing in Wan2.7, and Wan3.0 carries it forward.

Getting Started

To use Wan3.0-Video, you need a DeepInfra account and an API key. DeepInfra applies a zero-retention policy to inputs and outputs.

Authentication

Create a key in the DeepInfra dashboard and pass it in the Authorization header of every request:

Authorization: Bearer <DEEPINFRA_API_KEY>

API endpoint basics

  • Base URL: https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/inference
  • Model path: /Wan-AI/Wan3.0-Video
  • HTTP method: POST
  • Content type: application/json

Making your first API call

The example below generates a short video with Python.

import os
import requests
 
url = "https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/inference/Wan-AI/Wan3.0-Video"
headers = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['DEEPINFRA_API_KEY']}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}
 
payload = {
    "prompt": "A cinematic drone shot flying over a misty pine forest at sunrise",
    "duration": 5,
    "resolution": "720P",
    "audio": True,
    "prompt_extend": True,
}
 
response = requests.post(url, headers=headers, json=payload)
print(response.json()["video_url"])copy

To guide a generation with reference media, add a media array. Refer to each asset in the prompt as Image 1, Video 1, and so on, numbered in the order the assets appear in the array.

payload = {
    "prompt": "Image 1 walks through a rainy neon street at night",
    "media": [
        {"type": "reference_image", "url": "https://example.com/character.png"}
    ],
    "duration": 8,
}copy

Configuration and Parameters

Each request needs either a prompt or media.

Common parameters

ParameterTypeDefaultDescription
promptstringEmptyText description of the video. Use Image n or Video n to reference assets in the media array.
mediaarrayEmptyInput media objects, each with a type and a url.
durationinteger5Video length from 2 to 30 seconds. Set -1 for a model-chosen duration.
resolutionstring1080POutput tier: 480P, 720P, or 1080P.
ratiostringadaptiveAspect ratio such as 16:9 or 9:16. Adaptive derives the ratio from input media.
audiobooleantrueGenerates a synchronized audio track.
prompt_extendbooleantrueRewrites the prompt to improve output quality.
watermarkbooleanfalseAdds an AI-generated watermark.
seedintegerNoneValue from 0 to 2147483647 for reproducible outputs.

Media entries use one of these types: first_frame, last_frame, reference_image, reference_video, reference_audio, file, or link. Reference types cannot be combined with first_frame or last_frame. When a request includes a reference_video, the input and output durations together must stay within 30 seconds.

Input limits

Input typeLimitFormats and notes
Text prompt20,000 charactersDescribes the scene, motion, and audio
Reference images10 imagesJPEG, PNG, BMP, and WEBP, up to 20 MB each
Reference videos5 clips, 15 seconds totalMP4 and MOV, up to 100 MB each
Reference audio5 clips, 15 seconds totalWAV and MP3, up to 15 MB each
Documents1 file, up to 50 pagesPDF, DOCX, PPTX, and Markdown, up to 100 MB
Web links1 linkPublic URLs that do not require a login

Response Format

The API returns a JSON payload with a link to the generated video. An inference_status object reports the status, runtime, and cost of the request.

{
  "video_url": "https://example.com/video.mp4",
  "request_id": null,
  "inference_status": {
    "status": "succeeded",
    "runtime_ms": 0,
    "cost": 0.0
  }
}copy

Pricing

Wan3.0-Video is billed at $0.20 per second of generated video. A 10-second clip costs $2.00, and a 30-second clip costs $6.00. DeepInfra lists the rate per second of generated output.

Conclusion

Wan3.0-Video combines omni-modal input with audio and video output in one model. Creators can turn text, images, and documents into finished video without assembling a multi-model pipeline.

  • Range: Generates up to 30 seconds of video with integrated audio and multi-modal references.
  • Control: Offers prompt_extend, adaptive aspect ratios, seeds, and optional watermarks.
  • Simple billing: Charges a single per-second rate for generated video.

DeepInfra also hosts other video models that accept reference inputs, such as ByteDance Seedance 2.0, so you can compare outputs through the same API.

Related articles

Reliable JSON-Only Responses with DeepInfra LLMs<p>When large language models are used inside real applications, their role changes fundamentally. Instead of chatting with users, they become infrastructure components: extracting information, transforming text, driving workflows, or powering APIs. In these scenarios, natural language is no longer the desired output. What applications need is structured data — and very often, that structure is […]</p>

GLM-5.3 Model Overview & Integration Guide<p>GLM-5.3 is a large-scale reasoning model from Z.ai, built for complex software engineering and long-horizon agent tasks. It handles text input and output across a 1,048,576-token context window, and is one of several hundred models in DeepInfra’s catalog. The model uses the same base as GLM-5.2. Every gain comes from post-training, which is where Z.ai […]</p>

Nemotron 3 Nano vs GPT-OSS-20B: Performance, Benchmarks & DeepInfra Results<p>The open-source LLM landscape is becoming increasingly diverse, with models optimized for reasoning, throughput, cost-efficiency, and real-world agentic applications. Two models that stand out in this new generation are NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Nano and OpenAI’s GPT-OSS-20B, both of which offer strong performance while remaining openly available and deployable across cloud and edge systems. Although both […]</p>

item.title: [AI21 Labs] How we cut GitLab Duo Code Review’s cost by 98%
item.content:encoded:
In Brief

We cut GitLab Duo Code Review’s cost by 98% on Martian’s Code Review Bench without losing review quality, and all of it came from optimizing the harness: which model each stage runs on and how much context each stage reads. Neither change gets there alone. The open-weight model stalled on a handful of oversized reviews, and compacting the context is what made them fit.

Figure 1. Cost against F1 for every setup in the results table. F1 stays within two points of the baseline throughout. The same compaction step saves 19% from the baseline and 84% after the model switch; on a log axis, arrow length reflects the percentage saved.

An agent’s cost is eventually set by its harness: which stages it runs, what each stage reads, and which model does the work. We took GitLab Duo Code Review, whose harness is source available, measured where its money sits, and, with our own agent helping run the experiments, changed one thing at a time until the bill stopped dropping.

But the real story is not the final changes in the harness; it’s the way we got there. Switching to a smaller model in every stage hurt the quality. Moving to an open-weight model on every stage cut 85% of the cost, but we didn’t stop there. While compaction looks marginal at first glance, the 98% only shows up with both, because the open-weight model’s deployment window decides which requests it can take at all. The model sets the price. The harness decides whether you get to use it.

We ran this on public pull requests, with no GitLab production traffic or customer data. Quality is F1 on one public benchmark, scored by two judges. Cost is token spend at published list prices, including for the model we serve ourselves, so it measures what the harness consumes. What our own infrastructure costs is a separate question. Configurations were chosen and tuned on the same 50 pull requests they’re scored on, so read these as measured results on this benchmark; how they hold on a new codebase is untested. The full methodology is at the end.

A pipeline with four stages

Duo Code Review, the Code Review Flow of GitLab Duo Agent Platform, reviews merge requests and posts comments. At the time of testing, it ran Claude Sonnet 5 by default, and GitLab published the flow, built on LangGraph, in its source-available ai-assist repository. That, plus a public benchmark, is why we chose it.

It runs four model stages, each with its own prompt and at most two tools:

  • Exploration lists the repository tree around the changed files.
  • File fetching reads related files: tests, callers, custom instructions.
  • Analysis turns what was fetched into notes.
  • Review reads the diff and most changed files in full, then posts comments.

Figure 2. Duo Code Review’s four stages. Each starts from a fresh prompt with at most two tools.

Every generic optimization we had built targets coding agents like Claude Code, which resend one growing conversation full of tool output and tool definitions. Duo Code Review’s stages are independent: each starts with a fresh prompt, carries at most two tools, and has no history to trim. Our defaults had nothing to act on and changed zero requests.

It turns out there’s no one-size-fits-all approach to harness optimization; each harness requires its own careful analysis.

Where the money goes

Figure 3. Where the baseline’s $0.589 per PR goes. The review is 65% of the bill, split almost evenly between what it reads and how much it reasons.

The review is 65% of the bill, and its output alone is a third of the total: free to think before it posts, Sonnet 5 writes about 18,600 tokens per review, nearly all reasoning. Exploration and fetching, which only decide which files to read, are 27%. Analysis is 9%.

The money mainly goes in three places: the context every stage reads, the mechanical stages, and the review’s reasoning. No single change reaches all three but each step below reaches one of them.

Finding 1: less context, more reasoning

Can we cut what the review reads without hurting it? Yes, and it saves less than arithmetic suggests.

The review stage builds its context including changed files in full, plus a diff where every line sits in a tag repeating its type and both line numbers. A unified diff marks the same line with one character.

We compacted both in front of the flow, with rules rather than a model: nothing is summarized. File windowing keeps each changed hunk plus 25 lines either side of both the old and new line ranges, and elides the rest. Diff compaction rewrites the per-line diff as a standard unified diff with the same hunks and line numbers.

The median review prompt fell from 59K to 32K tokens. Spending on review context fell further, by 62%, because the largest prompts shrank hardest.

Yet the review’s cost fell by only a fifth. With compaction on, Sonnet 5 also wrote more: about 23,800 output tokens per review instead of 18,600, nearly all reasoning. We haven’t isolated why, but it caps what compaction can save on its own. On its own, compaction took cost from $0.589 to $0.475, a 19.4% saving, at 47.2% F1 and 1.16x the latency.

Figure 4. Baseline against compaction. Spending on the review’s context falls 62%, but its reasoning output grows 28%, so the bill falls only 19%.

Finding 2: the open-weight model held on every stage

How far does changing models get you? That depends on which stage you change.

We started by moving Claude Haiku 4.5 onto one stage at a time. On exploration and fetching, it picked the same files Sonnet 5 did. Early tests on the other two were less kind: quality dipped with Haiku on analysis and dropped sharply with it on the review. Same model, very different results depending on where it sat. Kept on the two mechanical stages, Haiku cut the bill 15.4% at unchanged F1, and 34.6% with compaction.

That was as far as Haiku could go. It couldn’t hold quality on the review, where most of the money is, and at half Sonnet 5’s price it wouldn’t have moved the bill enough if it had. Reaching the review’s reasoning meant leaving the Claude family.

We then turned to an open-weight model: DeepSeek V4 Flash, the first one we tried, which we serve with vLLM on H100s. At Together AI’s list price it costs 14x less than Sonnet 5 per input token and 36x less per output token. With all four stages on it and compaction off, cost fell to $0.086, an 85.3% saving, at 48.4% F1 and 0.37x the latency. On this benchmark it held on every stage, review included.

Two harness settings made that hold. Reasoning effort was set by measurement (see “What didn’t help”). And about one review call in seven on DeepSeek ended without posting; GitLab’s own correction step retried each one, so every review was posted, and the retries are in the costs.

Why the saving stopped at 85%

Our DeepSeek deployment accepts prompts up to 256K tokens; anything longer stays on Sonnet 5 so the review completes. The model supports 1M, but serving that window takes a more complex deployment, and its quality at very long contexts is still debated. Without compaction, some review prompts reach 480K, and 3 of the 50 PRs cross the limit, producing 11 fallback calls.

Figure 5. With every stage on the open-weight model and no compaction, 3 of 50 PRs (6%) exceed the 256K deployment and fall back to Sonnet 5. Those 11 calls carry 77% of the remaining $0.086 per PR.

Six percent of pull requests carried 77% of what was left. And the prompts that overflow are the largest reviews, large for exactly the reasons in Finding 1.

So compaction goes back in, this time to make prompts fit. The largest review prompt drops from 480K to 109K. Every review fits. Nothing falls back. Cost reaches $0.0135 per PR, 97.7% below baseline, at 47.2% F1 and 0.35x the latency, with the second judge within half a point.

Figure 6. Cost per PR along the way. The best setup on Claude reaches $0.385, the open-weight model on every stage reaches $0.086, and adding compaction brings it to $0.0135: 98% below baseline, at 47.2% F1 against 46.4%.

At that point compaction’s own token saving is about $0.006 per PR. What it buys is fit. In front of Claude, compaction is a cost optimization. In front of a 256K deployment, it keeps every review on the open-weight model.

A 1M deployment would also have removed the fallback. It would not have shrunk what every review reads, and it would have leaned on the model at the lengths where its quality is least settled.

What didn’t help

What we triedWhat we found
Raising reasoning effortAt “max” on 30 trial reviews, recall rose from 38.9% to 52.8% while F1 moved from 35.0% to 35.4%, at 3.5x the latency: more findings, more cost, no better reviews
Prompt cachingLittle to reuse. Requests within a stage share their instructions, but the stages share no prefix with each other, so the diff and files every stage reads can’t be reused across stages
A lower-priced model for exploration and fetchingNot worth testing. In the final setup those stages cost $0.005 of $0.0135 per PR, so even a free model would add about one point to the saving

Results

SetupF1Cost per PRCost vs baseline
Staying on Claude
Baseline: Sonnet 5 on every stage46.4%$0.5890%
Compaction only47.2%$0.475−19.4%
Haiku 4.5 for exploration and fetching46.3%$0.498−15.4%
Haiku 4.5 for exploration and fetching, plus compaction46.0%$0.385−34.6%
Adding the open-weight model
DeepSeek for exploration and fetching, plus compaction45.9%$0.370−37.1%
DeepSeek for everything except the review, plus compaction45.1%$0.317−46.1%
DeepSeek on every stage48.4%$0.086−85.3%
DeepSeek on every stage, plus compaction47.2%$0.0135−97.7%

Any stage not named runs on Sonnet 5. No setup moved F1 by more than 2 points on either judge. The final setup’s reviews are more precise than the baseline’s (46.8% vs 41.9%) but catch slightly fewer issues (recall 47.6% vs 52.0%), and at about 9,000 tokens against 18,600, run at about a third of the latency.

Summary

  • The bill sat in three places, each needing a different change: shared context, mechanical stages, and the review’s reasoning.
  • Haiku 4.5 held quality on the two mechanical stages and lost it on analysis and the review.
  • With compaction, the median review prompt shrank 46% while reasoning output grew 28%.
  • Three of 50 PRs carried 77% of the remaining cost until compaction made every review fit the deployment’s window.

Compaction on its own is worth 19.4%. Added after the model change, the same compaction is worth 84% of what was left, because by then its job was making prompts fit.

That interdependence is what makes harness optimization hard, and why it pays off. The settings in this study kept changing each other’s value. Compaction was worth a fifth of the bill on Sonnet 5 and decided the outcome on a 256K deployment. Haiku was safe on two stages and hurt quality on the other two. Getting to 98% meant searching configurations as a whole, and that search is where the saving came from.

The specific settings belong to this agent, and they’re already dated: GitLab has moved Duo Code Review to Sonnet 5.5 since we ran this. The method travels better. Measure cost per stage before changing anything. Change one variable at a time, and re-test earlier changes after each new one lands. Most teams won’t have a public benchmark to work against; we’d expect the same loop to work on a slice of live traffic, and once a configuration holds on most of it, it becomes a line in the harness.

Appendix: How we measured

Everything in the table below was fixed before the first run. Our own agent helped run the search inside those rules, proposing, executing, and scoring configurations.

What we tested onMartian’s Code Review Bench, full offline set: 50 real pull requests from Sentry, Grafana, Cal.com, Discourse, and Keycloak, with 173 human-verified “golden” comments, the issues a good review should catch
How a review is scoredA judge model matches the agent’s comments to the golden ones. Precision: how many of its comments match. Recall: how many golden comments it found. F1 balances the two. Claude Opus 4.5 judges with Martian’s prompts, GPT-5.2 as a cross-check
What “comparable” meansEach configuration reviews each PR 3 times. Comparable means F1 is less than 5 points below baseline even at the pessimistic end of its 95% confidence interval, on both judges
How cost is pricedPublished prices per million input/output tokens, no caching discount: Sonnet 5 2/10, Haiku 4.5 1/5. We self-host DeepSeek V4 Flash, so we price it at Together AI’s public rate, 0.14/0.28, instead of our own serving cost
BaselineThe agent as shipped, Sonnet 5 on every stage: 46.4% F1, $0.589 per PR (code_review flow 2.0.0, ai-assist commit 5272972)

To check our scoring, we ran it on GitLab’s own recorded reviews of these PRs, which Martian publishes: 52.3% F1 against Martian’s 54.2%. Those came from a different configuration, so they validate our scoring and tell us nothing about our baseline. These are public PRs, so their content may have been in training data. What we can rule out is the review models reproducing the answers from the question: given only each PR’s title, URL, and commit link, both score about 4% F1. Every file the agent read came from pinned offline copies.

Thanks to GitLab’s team for publishing the Duo Code Review flow and its benchmark results, which made this study possible.

item.title: [Modular (原 BentoCloud/BentoML)] Modular: MAX is now source available and open to everyone
item.content:encoded:
October 22, 2026

MAX is now source available and open to everyone

Modular Team

Product

Today, we're excited to announce a major milestone for Modular: the complete MAX source code is now publicly available, alongside a radically simplified MAX License.

Developers can now explore, modify, and extend the entire MAX stack. Building on our open source kernels, models, and serving infrastructure, this release opens the remaining core components that power MAX's heterogeneous capabilities: the graph compiler, runtime, and hardware backends. These include support for CPUs and GPUs.

Under the new license, you can build and distribute commercial products with MAX without licensing fees or royalties. We’re also opening MAX to community contributions, starting with bug fixes and expanding over time. We’re also actively supercharging MAX with agentic infrastructure development that will increase our overall development approach.

This milestone builds on our progressive approach to opening our stack. We started with the Mojo standard library in 2024, followed by MAX's kernels, models, serving infrastructure, and APIs throughout 2025. In August of this year, we fully open sourced the entire Mojo compiler and toolchain. Today, we complete the picture by making the remaining MAX compiler, runtime, and hardware backends source available.

As Modular enters a new chapter within Qualcomm, we’re accelerating our mission to democratize heterogeneous compute. In the next few months, we will launch an alliance program, with a goal of uniting developers and hardware vendors around a single software platform. Opening MAX is the first step toward that shared ecosystem.

The new MAX License

We designed the new MAX License to balance two priorities: enabling the community to build with more flexibility, and balancing the long-term sustainability of MAX and its ecosystem.

That starts with giving developers the freedom to build. You can use, modify, extend, and build commercial products with MAX, without licensing fees or royalties. Our goal is to remove barriers to adoption and give developers, researchers, and hardware vendors the freedom to innovate on top of the entire stack.

Equally important is ensuring that the ecosystem can thrive over the long term. Our team has spent decades building and maintaining major open source projects, and we've seen the challenges they face. Fragmentation is a common pitfall, especially for foundational infrastructure like MAX. MAX’s core goal is to unify the programming model across hardware, and that goal becomes much harder to achieve if every platform develops its own incompatible version.

We designed the license with these considerations in mind. As with Mojo, we expect our approach to continue evolving as the technology matures and we hear more from the community.

What the MAX License covers

Many MAX components are already open source under Apache 2.0. These include the MAX kernel library in Mojo, Mojo interfaces for programming accelerators, Python APIs for the serving CLI and modeling, MAX models, and more. All of these components will remain under Apache 2.0.

The new MAX License covers the MAX internals we’re making source available today, plus the MAX binaries we distribute. Each source file includes a header identifying the license that applies to it.

Here’s what the MAX License allows:

  • Unlimited MAX usage on any hardware, without licensing fees: Build with MAX on any hardware, for free.
  • Contribute back to MAX: Fork MAX for the purposes of contributing back to the main MAX project.
  • Build libraries and applications on top of MAX: Create projects and libraries using MAX and license them however you choose. Components of MAX, such as the kernels (Apache 2.0), the graph compiler (MAX License), and device backends (MAX License), retain their licenses and you can license your code as you see fit.

There a few limitations:

  • AI-assisted reimplementation of MAX: You can't use any part of MAX as input to an AI system to produce a reimplementation of MAX. We want to build a community and pull people together, not be the foundation for many AI-driven forks.
  • Commercial hosted inference services: If you use MAX for hosted inference or training services that you sell to customers, you must prominently display the “Modular Accelerated” wordmark on your product to recognize our contribution to your commercial products.
  • Publication and distribution of modified source code: You can't publish or distribute modified MAX source code, except by forking MAX for the purpose of contributing changes back to the main project. We know that there are many fierce competitors in the AI landscape, and hope to replicate LLVM’s success of getting people to build on a shared codebase that can service many different companies' needs, better than any one can build for themself.

Our intent is to encourage experimentation and innovation while ensuring that MAX continues to evolve as a unified software foundation. Developers are free to modify and experiment with MAX, and we want to make it as easy as possible to contribute improvements back to the project. The license’s distribution restrictions are designed to prevent fragmentation into incompatible versions of MAX, not to discourage individual developers from exploring new ideas. We recognize that there are many legitimate reasons to experiment with modifications that aren’t ready for upstream contribution, and we’ll continue working with the community to make sure our development and contribution processes support that innovation.

MAX may also collect usage telemetry to help us improve the product. We handle personal information in accordance with our Privacy Policy, which describes users’ rights under applicable data protection laws, including the EU and UK GDPR and the California Consumer Privacy Act. As with most software licenses, MAX is provided as-is, without warranties.

For more details on the MAX License, explore the FAQ and read the full license.

What comes next

With the full MAX codebase now source available, we’re also opening MAX to community contributions starting today. Initially, we’ll accept bug fixes, with plans to expand to refactors and other changes over time, following the same gradual approach we took with the Mojo standard library and compiler.

Our next step is to bring MAX and Mojo to the broader AI ecosystem. At ModCon, we announced the Modular alliance program, bringing together hardware vendors, model labs, and data center operators around a common software foundation.

Partners who contribute engineering resources, compute, or early model checkpoints will help shape the future of MAX, with a voice in governance and conformance standards, input into the roadmap, priority for upstream contributions, early access to model checkpoints, ownership of dedicated hardware backends, and more permissive licensing.

We’ll share more about the alliance in the coming months. If you’re interested in getting involved, reach out at alliance@modular.com.

To learn more about the new MAX License, join Modular cofounders Chris Lattner and Tim Davis for a live Q&A on November 10 at 10 AM PT. RSVP here.

Get started

  • Browse the MAX source on GitHub
  • Read the full MAX License
  • Read the MAX License FAQ
  • Install MAX with pip install max[all]
  • Check out the contributor guide to submit a bug fix
  • Build MAX from source
  • Share your feedback on the Modular forum or in Discord

We look forward to seeing what you build with MAX. If any part of the license remains unclear, we want to hear from you. Your feedback shaped this release, and it will continue to guide the steps that follow.

Read more from Modular

item.title: [Modular (原 BentoCloud/BentoML)] Modular: Modular 26.7: Opening up MAX
item.content:encoded:
October 22, 2026

Modular 26.7: Opening up MAX

Modular Team

Product

The headline of Modular 26.7 is one we've wanted to write for a long time: this release opens the MAX graph compiler, MAX runtime, and device extensibility hooks for everyone. This means that MAX is now fully source-available, and can be built and modified by hardware innovators, researchers, and everyone else who loves making accelerators go "brr." This release also brings an eager mode that gets you debugging custom ops in a fraction of the time, decision model support, and the next step in Mojo's growth into a systems programming language.

MAX is now fully source-available

At our recent ModCon conference, we committed to opening up MAX, and we're delivering on that promise.

The full source for MAX is now available: hardware backends, the graph compiler, the runtime, and more. Our new MAX License is intentionally permissive: you can use, modify, extend, and build commercial products with MAX, without licensing fees or royalties. If you've wanted to bring up MAX on your own accelerator, this is where to start, and you can see the existing implementation for NVIDIA, AMD, Apple Silicon, and CPUs as a reference point. We plan to release source for the MAX plugins for other chips, including Qualcomm Dragonfly and Google TPU, in the coming months.

Why not Apache 2.0?

The MAX License allows nearly everything Apache 2.0 does: use, modify, extend, and build commercial products with MAX, with no fees or royalties. The difference comes down to fragmentation. We’ve spent decades maintaining major open source projects and have seen the challenges they face. MAX aims to unify the programming model across hardware, and incompatible platform-specific versions would undermine that goal. The Modular alliance program is how we solve this, giving hardware vendors and partners a shared path to build on MAX without splintering the ecosystem. As with Mojo, we expect our approach to evolve as the technology matures and we hear from the community.

There's far more in the MAX source code than we can cover here, so we wrote a separate post on what's included and what you can build with it.

What's new in MAX

Eager mode for faster development

MAX has long had an advanced graph compiler that performs automatic fusion and other optimizations for peak performance. But during development, fast iteration often matters more than peak performance. MAX now has full eager mode support, including your custom ops, and it shares a single code path with the graph compiler, so the code you run in eager mode is the same as what you compile and ship.

Declare an op once, call it directly on a Tensor, then reuse it unchanged inside a compiled Module. That makes the development loop much faster: on a slice of Gemma 4 31B, eager mode reaches the first token in about 30 seconds, compared to about 110 seconds compiled.

Here’s an example of how eager mode works with custom ops:

python

n, w, c = custom.Symbols("n", "w", "c")
downsample = custom.declare(
    "downsample",
    inputs={"x": custom.TemplateType(DType.float32, [n, w, c])},
    outputs=[custom.TemplateType(DType.float32, [n, w // 2, c])],
    custom_extensions=["path/to/kernels"],
)

# Eager: runs immediately.
y = downsample(Tensor.ones([2, 8, 3]))        # shape (2, 4, 3)

# Compiled: same op inside a Module.
class Encoder(Module):
    def forward(self, x: Tensor) -> Tensor:
        return downsample(x) * 2.0

model = Encoder().compile(TensorType(DType.float32, ["batch", 8, 3], device=Encoder().device))
y = model(Tensor.ones([2, 8, 3]))             # same op, now compiled

Support for System One/decision models, new modalities, and more models

There’s been a lot of recent excitement about the new modality of System One/decision models, due to their ability to enable zero-shot classification in a very inexpensive manner. MAX has added initial support for these decision models, including Decider 2B, through the new v1/decisions and v1/systemone API endpoints.

MAX has also added support for MiMo-V2.6-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, and Muse-Glimmer, with KDA and sparse MLA.

In addition to new capabilities, we continue to improve existing model families. Several ops that used to round-trip through the CPU now run entirely on the GPU, which gives a 2.6x prefill speedup for Qwen and GLM models.

Mojo 1.2: growing into a systems language

With 1.0, Mojo proved itself as a language for high-performance code across heterogeneous hardware. Now we're leaning into the next phase of the Mojo roadmap: Mojo as a systems programming language.

Pattern matching

Mojo 1.2's flagship new feature is pattern matching. The match statement lets you replace long chains of conditionals with clear, structured cases, and the compiler can check that you've handled every one of them.

python

def classify_point(p: Tuple[Int, Int]) -> String:
    match p:
        case 0, 0:
            return "origin"
        case x, 0 if x < 0:
            return String("negative x-axis:", x)
        case x, 0:
            return String("x-axis:", x)
        case 0, y:
            return String("y-axis:", y)
        case x, y:
            return String("point:", x, ",", y)

As a bonus, it also works at compile-time:

python

def classify_type[T: AnyType]() -> String:
    comptime match T:
        case == Int:
            return "integer"
        case == String:
            return "string"
        case _:
            return "other"

More expressive traits and constraints

Structs can now explicitly opt out of trait conformance (for example, by declaring themselves not Movable), and where clauses accept an else branch so you can state exactly why a constraint failed. Both make generic code easier to read and easier to debug.

See the Mojo changelog for the full list of changes in 1.2.

Get started

  • Upgrade with pip install --upgrade max
  • Read the MAX License blog post and FAQ
  • Explore the full MAX 26.7 changelog
  • Check out the full Mojo 1.2 changelog

With the whole stack open, we can’t wait to see what you build. Share it on the Modular forum.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Physicist Christopher Stubbs joins Anthropic's Long-Term Ben…
item.description: Full title: Physicist Christopher Stubbs joins Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust
item.content:encoded:
Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, has joined Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust. He brings to the Trust decades of scientific expertise across observational cosmology and precision measurement. He has also advised the US government on national security and arms control.

“I am honored to join Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust and to help the company deliver on its public benefit mission,” said Stubbs. “I use AI tools in my research every day and see what they make possible, and as an educator I have confronted some of the hard questions they raise. As a grandfather, I want to help ensure that AI is developed and deployed for the long-term benefit of humanity.”

Stubbs is the Samuel C. Moncher Professor of Physics and of Astronomy at Harvard, where he served as Dean of Science from 2018 to 2024. In 1998, as a member of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, he helped discover the accelerating expansion of the universe, work that later earned the team the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. He was also the inaugural project scientist for what is now the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which started a 10-year survey of the southern sky in June. One of its aims is to study the accelerating expansion he helped discover.

More recently, he’s written about how to keep AI-assisted research reproducible when models can give different answers to the same question. He’s a member of JASON, an independent group of scientists who have advised the US government on defense and technology since 1960.

“When Chris found evidence that the universe was expanding at a rate no one expected, he and his team followed the data even when it went against the prevailing wisdom of the field. As AI starts to transform how science itself is done, Chris’s intellectual honesty, rigor, and commitment to the truth are the values we want shaping the future of this technology, and I’m grateful he’s bringing his deep expertise to the Trust,” said Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic.

Anthropic is a Public Benefit Corporation, which means we’re structured to balance commercial growth with our public benefit purpose. The Trust exists to help us hold that balance over the long term. It has the authority to appoint a majority of Anthropic’s board, and Trustees advise the board and our leadership on critical decisions, particularly those involving risks and societal impacts of AI.

This week we published our first Public Benefit Report, a public account of how we’re working toward our charter and where we’re falling short. The Trustees helped define the five charter pillars it measures us against, and the report closes with their assessment of our progress to date. Subject to stockholder approval, we’ve also committed to setting aside a portion of Anthropic’s shares to Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows.

“Helping the world build powerful AI safely and making sure it meaningfully improves people’s lives both depend on a deep understanding of science and on leading with integrity,” added Neil Buddy Shah, Chair of the Long-Term Benefit Trust. “Not only has Chris worked on some of the hardest problems in science, but he has consistently been a high-integrity leader of large, complex, collaborative scientific endeavors across academia, government, and the national laboratories. That will be of great value to the Trust as we support Anthropic in developing AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.”

Stubbs, the Trust’s first physicist, joins Shah, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and former Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke. Trustees are independent of the company’s management and investors.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] HCLTech joins the Claude Partner Network as a Global Premier…
item.description: Full title: HCLTech joins the Claude Partner Network as a Global Premier partner
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic is partnering with HCLTech (opens in new tab), a global technology company with more than 230,000 people in 60 countries. HCLTech will build agentic solutions on Claude for its clients through a dedicated Anthropic Business Unit and Center of Excellence, embed Claude in HCLSoftware products, and integrate Claude and Claude Code into AI Force, the platform it uses to run IT services for clients. HCLTech becomes a Global Premier Partner (opens in new tab) in the Claude Partner Network.

HCLTech provides solutions for financial services, manufacturing, life sciences and healthcare, technology, semiconductor, telecom and media, retail and CPG, and mobility and public services. In these environments, a mistake is expensive and every change needs to be reviewed, logged, and approved. The partnership is built to put Claude into that work with the controls designed for those environments.

How HCLTech is putting Claude to work

HCLTech is bringing Claude into its business in three places and is designing each with guardrails and human review.

  • A dedicated Anthropic Business Unit and Center of Excellence. HCLTech’s forward-deployed engineers will set up secure sandbox environments where clients can test Claude against their own systems and data before deploying. The Center will train client workforces, help engineering teams adopt AI-native practices, and build the organizational controls for running agents safely at scale.
  • Claude inside HCLSoftware products. HCLSoftware becomes an Anthropic independent software vendor (ISV) partner and will embed Claude in select products across cybersecurity, automation, business process applications, and application development. The first are HCL BigFix for endpoint management, HCL AppScan for application security testing, and the Actian AI analyst for data and analytics.
  • Claude and Claude Code in AI Force. AI Force is how HCLTech delivers IT support, code remediation, and digital employee services for the enterprises it serves. Claude and Claude Code go into that platform with policy guardrails, exception handling, and human oversight for high-impact changes. Agents handle the routine work, and HCLTech engineers review and approve anything that touches a client’s production systems.

“Few technology companies combine the scale of a global systems integrator with the product depth of an ISV,” says C Vijayakumar, CEO and Managing Director at HCLTech. “That gives us a rare advantage to securely engineer and deploy Agentic AI at scale and deliver the business outcomes that matter most to our clients. Our partnership with Anthropic further strengthens our capabilities to achieve the same.”

"AI can only be as useful as it is trustworthy, and we build Claude to give companies the confidence to bring it into their most sensitive and valuable work,” says Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President at Anthropic. “HCLTech manages those kinds of systems for banks, hospitals, telecom companies and manufacturers, and we’re excited to partner with them as they integrate Claude and Claude Code. This partnership — and our broader commitment to advancing capability and safety together — is how AI will change the way entire industries run for the better.”

To learn more about working with Anthropic partners, visit the Claude Partner Network (opens in new tab).

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Introducing Claude Duet
item.content:encoded:
Today, we’re opening a research preview of Claude Duet, a new app where Claude works as a proactive agent. It comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working even when you step away, and checks with you before it acts on your behalf. We built Claude Duet for professionals and small business owners with more on their plates than they can track.

It’s available as a standalone app on iOS and Android, and on claude.ai. For this research preview, Claude Duet is included in Pro and Max plans and uses the same usage limits as the rest of Claude. To get access, join the waitlist (opens in new tab).

Put your attention where it matters most

We designed Claude Duet to be a partner you can trust. Professionals of all kinds have to juggle many decisions a day, and we think they’ll find Claude Duet most useful. It helps you prioritize where to spend your time and energy, and to leave room for the ambitious projects that felt impossible or daunting before.

What makes Claude Duet so helpful is its judgment. We designed it around Claude Opus 5.5 (opens in new tab) and built it to be resourceful and to decide what needs you, what can wait, and when to check with you first.

Each morning, it sends you a short brief on the most important items across your connected apps. Throughout the day, it keeps tabs on those apps and messages you only when something needs your attention. You can also hand it tasks of all shapes—from simple administrative tasks of scheduling meetings to more complex ones, such as building dashboards with dozens of tools, creating financial or sales forecasts, prototyping, and building web apps.

Safety and discretion are built in

Claude Duet draws on years of security, safety, and privacy work on agents, both our own and the infrastructure businesses use to run theirs:

  • Claude Duet draws on our framework for trustworthy agents (opens in new tab), which also guides agents like Claude Code and Claude in Chrome.
  • Claude Duet’s handling of credentials follows the design we use for Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab), so it never directly sees your passwords or sign-in tokens.
  • Actions are approved by our auto mode classifier (opens in new tab), the same safeguard that protects Claude and Claude Code from taking steps you didn’t ask for.
  • Claude Duet’s defenses against hidden instructions and prompt injection come from our browser-use research (opens in new tab), and our models and safeguards also cover this more broadly.
  • We run adversarial tests for Claude Duet’s security infrastructure. Red teams and an external firm penetration tested Claude Duet, and it’s covered by our public bug bounty program (opens in new tab).

How Duet handles sensitive information. We’re also releasing Claude Duet with a new dedicated classifier and safety system prompt that checks each message and guards against leaks of sensitive information. An agent that reads email and sends messages for you is constantly deciding where information should go. This new classifier and prompt are designed to reject requests to share the strictest tier of information, including credit card numbers and government identification. Other sensitive information, such as health or personal finances, are let through only when you’ve explicitly instructed Claude Duet to send it.

We’re continuing to develop and strengthen these protections, and will share more details about how Claude Duet is designed for safety in the coming days.

How testers are using Claude Duet

People at Anthropic have been using Claude Duet to accomplish more, but also to leave more room for thinking and being present. Boris Cherny, who leads our Claude Code team, talks through his mental to-do list with Claude Duet on walks, instead of saving the work for his desk. Chelsea Larsson, who leads our model and product behavior design team, hands Claude Duet her to-do list before leaving to be with her kids and it saves the results for an evening report. And the team behind Claude Duet uses it to build the product. Karan Ahuja, who leads the team, works with it to schedule user interviews, partner with him on prototypes, and even ship code.

We gave small business owners and entrepreneurs early access to Claude Duet, and some have been using it to help run their businesses. Here’s what some of them said:

Jess gets a rundown from Claude Duet each morning. One day, without being asked, it flagged a property showing that was on her calendar for the wrong day. “[This is] exactly the kind of thing I want caught without having to ask,” she said.

Jess Provencher, broker and owner, Pro Homes

Amin owns Shahs of Kabob in South Florida with about 110 employees. He’s used Claude Duet for accounting, customer support, and marketing, and has worked through his invoices store by store. “It brings it all together,” he said. “I don’t need to open up 100 tabs.”

Amin Ebrahimi, owner, Shahs of Kabob

Mya had a call coming up with a potential client. Claude Duet saw it on her calendar and prepared a brief. It also noticed the call fell right before her flight and offered to move it. “I didn’t realize that it was right before my flight,” she said. “I love that proactivity.”

Mya Dalton, a brand strategist

How Claude Duet works

Your context from Claude is the foundation. Claude Duet carries over your memory, skills, and connected apps from your Claude account, so setting it up requires minimal work. What changes is how you work together: Claude Duet comes to you first, and you can message it through typing or voice in one ongoing thread, so a quick reply and a weeklong project both start in the same place.

Work continues when you step away. Claude Duet has a virtual machine with its own browser, so it doesn’t require your laptop or phone to be on. Describe a task in a short message, and it works out which apps to use and what steps to take in the background. You’ll receive a notification when the task is complete or needs your review.

Receive a message when something needs you. Claude Duet checks your connected accounts every few hours, because checking nonstop would use up your plan’s limits much faster. We’re continuing to test its judgment about when to message you, and we’ll keep tuning it based on what testers tell us. You can also tell it what you want to hear about and how often.

Important decisions stay with you. Claude Duet reads, drafts, and prepares work on its own. But before it sends a message, makes a payment, signs a document, or deletes anything, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your approval. A few things are off-limits even with your approval, like trading securities or moving money between accounts. You’re also able to disconnect any app Claude Duet has access to.

Connect with the tools your business runs on. Claude Duet can use the over 6,000 connectors and plugins in the Claude Marketplace (opens in new tab) to:

  • Find the Gmail and Slack messages you’ve missed and help you reply.
  • Check Intuit QuickBooks or Stripe for unpaid invoices and draft reminders.
  • Prepare and run payroll in Gusto, with hours, bonuses, and reimbursements filled in.
  • Draft a job posting and, once you edit and approve, post it to LinkedIn.
  • Help prepare agreements and send them for review and signature through Docusign.
  • Draft follow-up emails using the contact and deal history in HubSpot.
  • Turn your product launch into a social campaign in Canva.
  • Set up, design, and manage your Shopify store. Coming soon, a richer visual editor will let you design your storefront and preview it before anything goes live.

You can also use Claude Duet to purchase things for your business using Link, Stripe’s digital wallet. Claude Duet confirms the item with you, and Link asks you to approve the spend. It then pays with a virtual card, so your real card number isn’t shared. It can also use Shop Pay from Shopify to check out at online stores. Coming soon, with your permission, it will be able to sign in to sites with logins you’ve saved in 1Password.

Join the research preview

This is an early version of Claude Duet, and it still might misread a thread or miscalibrate what’s urgent. We built its core functionality around work, so personal errands, such as booking tickets, aren’t quite as strong, and it can’t yet show you its browser. For now, Claude Duet lives in its own app, separate from the main Claude app. What we learn from early users will shape how the two work together.

During the research preview, Claude Duet shares your plan’s usage limits with the rest of Claude, and it uses them differently than a typical conversation does. Its background checks count toward those limits, and larger tasks, like building a financial model or a deck, require more model turns and background work.

We’re starting today with Pro and Max users in the US. Join the waitlist (opens in new tab) and we’ll email as soon as Claude Duet’s ready for you.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Claude Security now scans continuously and tracks fixes
item.content:encoded:
Since Claude Security entered public beta in April, thousands of organizations have used it to find over a million vulnerabilities.

Instead of waiting for someone to start a scan, Claude Security now keeps up with your repositories as your code changes, keeps track of which findings get fixed, and uses what your team tells it about your environment to decide what matters. Claude Security is powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos, with no Cyber Verification Program access required.

The latest version of Claude Security is available today in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers. Organizations receive $25,000 in free usage credits each month, for two months. The offer applies to usage through December 31, 2026. You can view full terms in the Help Center.

Continuous monitoring keeps up with your code

A scan captures one moment, and code changes every day. Teams told us they wanted coverage that stays current without anyone having to schedule it.

Create a project, connect your repositories through the Claude GitHub app (including GitHub Enterprise Server) or with an access token from GitLab and other Git providers, and choose the branch and scope for each. Claude runs a deep baseline scan, then scans changes regularly based upon their risk and complexity, so your list of findings stays close to the current state of your code.

A project can hold multiple repositories, so Claude can catch issues that live between services, like a backend that trusts input a client was supposed to validate.

Findings are marked fixed when the fix ships

Most fixes happen outside the tool that found the issue. Claude Security checks open findings against the code that changed and marks them fixed when the fix lands, whether your team fixed it in Claude Code or in a separate process. If Claude Security finds the issue again later, the finding reopens automatically.

Your team’s knowledge shapes the scan

Every environment has controls a scanner can’t see from the code alone. Teams wanted a way to tell Claude Security about those controls, and to look across services that depend on each other. Now, each project has a knowledge base where you can describe how your code is deployed, which security policies apply, and anything a new security engineer on your team would need to know.

Claude Security also generates a threat model from your code that your team can review and edit. Subsequent scans use those threat models to decide what’s worth flagging. Added context also helps Claude Security skip risks your environment already handles.

Severity and exploit paths for every finding

Each finding comes with a severity rating, judged against your project’s threat model, and an explanation of how an attacker could reach the vulnerable code, so teams can fix what’s actually reachable first. Findings can include a diagram of the attack path.

Findings reach your tools, with controls for larger rollouts

The new API lets you integrate Claude Security into your existing workflows. You can list and read projects and findings, resolve or reopen findings, and create and manage projects and their repositories. Users can create a personal access token in Claude Security settings, and it can only see and change what the user can. Webhooks can also notify your systems when a new finding lands.

Claude Security is also available as an MCP connector in Claude.ai and Claude Code. An engineer can pull up a finding, ask Claude about it, start the fix, and mark it resolved in the same session.

New role-based access controls let admins decide who can view projects, triage findings, and create projects. Organizations can open Claude Security to more teams that own the code without giving everyone access to create projects.

Getting started

The latest version of Claude Security is available in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers starting today. Admins can enable it in the admin console and set who on their team can access it.

Use the Getting Started Guide to set up your first project, and visit the Help Center for more details.

Organizations receive $25,000 in free usage credits each month, for two months. The offer applies to usage through December 31, 2026. You can view full terms in the Help Center.

“Claude Security found many material issues that a traditional pen test conducted at the same time missed, several of which would have had significant impact if exploited in the wild.”

Jon Donovan, Software Engineer, IonQ

“Claude Security scanned our code once to set a baseline. Now it keeps up as our code changes, and our team fixes issues right in Claude instead of switching to another tool.”

Jake Meredith, Product Security, Gusto

“The API and MCP additions are a game changer and will be the path forward for IonQ’s Product Security team to further operationalize Claude Security.”

Joe Coniglio, Security Engineer, IonQ

“Claude Security found a number of logic flaws that none of our other tools had caught. Once we wrote our own risk policy into the threat model, focusing on what external users can actually reach, the findings matched how we prioritize instead of only a severity score”

item.title: [Mistral AI] Mistral Advances AI for Engineering with NVIDIA
item.content:encoded:
Company

Mistral Advances AI for Engineering with NVIDIA

October 21, 2026

By Mistral

5 min read

Copy url to clipboardCopied

Thinking

Summary

Mistral and NVIDIA are collaborating to revolutionize engineering workflows by integrating Mistral’s AI models with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and physics modeling tools, enabling faster simulations and closed-loop AI-driven design. The partnership will introduce public benchmarks and open datasets to standardize evaluations for physics and agentic AI in computer-aided engineering, while leveraging NVIDIA’s Omniverse for 3D simulation and asset creation. Building on their existing work, including the development of Mistral Large 4, the initiative aims to push the boundaries of AI-powered engineering across industries like aerospace, automotive, and semiconductors.

Mistral is collaborating with NVIDIA to develop a new generation of AI-native engineering workflows powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing. Combining Mistral Large 4, with Mistral’s data generation, and physics modeling pipelines, accelerated by NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries and NVIDIA Warp, the initiative aims to accelerate engineering simulation and enable closed-loop workflows that connect simulation, AI model development and engineering design. Mistral and NVIDIA will also work together to integrate Mistral's models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for GPU-accelerated 3D scene generation and SimReady asset creation.

A central focus of the collaboration is the development of public benchmarks and open datasets for evaluating physics models. These benchmarks will give researchers, developers and industrial teams a shared foundation to compare model accuracy and performance and build and validate automated CAD-to-simulation workflows.

"For too long, the pace of engineering has been set by the pace of simulation. With Mistral's open-weight models and physics AI capabilities, combined with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing stack, we’re giving engineers faster simulation cycles, as well as open benchmarks rigorous enough to validate agents on real CAE and EDA work.” Neil Ashton, VP of Computational Engineering, Mistral

Beyond physics AI, Mistral and NVIDIA will also work together to develop dedicated evaluations and benchmarks for agentic AI in computer-aided engineering (CAE) and electronic design automation (EDA) to accelerate the application of AI for engineering within aerospace, automotive and semiconductor use-cases. These benchmarks will assess agents’ ability to use engineering tools, complete multistep workflows and produce technically correct results, while measuring execution time and computational cost.

Through this work, Mistral and NVIDIA will help define standards for agentic and physics AI evaluations in engineering, establishing consistent, reproducible methods for assessing capabilities and tracking progress. Powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing, libraries and tools, Mistral will redefine AI for engineering, transforming how engineers design, simulate and build the next generation of products.

“The next wave of engineering breakthroughs will come from exploring ideas that were once too complex or time-consuming to test,” said Tim Costa, vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering at NVIDIA. “By combining Mistral’s advanced open models and deep expertise in physics AI with NVIDIA accelerated computing and libraries, we’re helping engineers push the boundaries of design—with shared industry benchmarks to build confidence in what AI can do.”

Building on the ongoing NVIDIA and Mistral partnership

The industrial engineering collaboration builds on an ongoing partnership between NVIDIA and Mistral spanning open model development, domain-specific AI and the infrastructure needed to bring these capabilities into production.

The companies previously co-developed Mistral NeMo and are now working together through the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition to develop a frontier base model that will continue to advance the open weight frontier. This shared foundation will enable developers and enterprises worldwide to specialize AI for their industries, languages and regions, supported by contributions of data, evaluations and domain expertise from coalition members.

Mistral recently introduced the public preview of Mistral Large 4, known as Le Chonk, its largest and most capable frontier model to date. With approximately 1 trillion total parameters and 49 billion active parameters, the multimodal model was trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral-operated data centers in Europe. It advances capabilities across coding, agentic workflows and multimodal understanding, with weights planned for release at the end of October.

Alongside model development, Mistral and NVIDIA are expanding the infrastructure that powers AI training, customization and inference. Mistral is bringing additional NVIDIA-powered AI infrastructure online in support of Mistral’s compute roadmap targeting 1 GW of capacity by 2030.

This expansion strengthens Europe’s role in developing and delivering AI for the world. By connecting European infrastructure and research with open models, specialized engineering capabilities and customer applications, Mistral and NVIDIA are helping enterprises build AI around their own expertise and scale it to serve markets worldwide.
